questions.stem: Which comparison between respirator fit testing and a user seal check is accurate?

options.text: Both are performed once a year by the employer's occupational health program using a test aerosol
Fit testing qualifies a specific make, model, and size before initial use and yearly after; a user seal check is done at every donning
A user seal check may substitute for fit testing as long as the wearer uses the same respirator model
Fit testing is repeated each time a respirator is donned, while a user seal check is completed once at the time of hire

rationales.whyCorrect: OSHA's Respiratory Protection standard, 29 CFR 1910.134, is federal law rather than a professional recommendation, and it requires that employees be fit tested before initial use of a tight-fitting respirator and at least annually thereafter. Fit testing establishes the particular make, model, style, and size that seals on that individual's face, and it uses a qualitative or quantitative protocol from Appendix A. The user seal check, described in the mandatory Appendix B-1, is a brief positive- and negative-pressure check the wearer performs every time the respirator is put on to confirm it is seated correctly that time. One qualifies the respirator to the person; the other verifies today's donning, and neither substitutes for the other.
rationales.eli10: Getting fit tested is like going to a shoe store and having someone measure your foot to learn you are a size 8 wide in that specific brand. You do not re-measure every morning, but you do check that the shoe is actually on right and laced before you run. That quick check is the user seal check: you cover the respirator, inhale and exhale, and feel whether air leaks around the edges. Measuring happens before your first use and at least once a year after that; the quick check happens every single time you put it on, because air always takes the easy path — if there is a gap at the edge, that is where it goes instead of through the filter.

questions.stem: A nurse removes a face shield by grasping the plastic across the front of the visor. What is the most likely consequence of this technique?

options.text: Contamination on the outer surface of the visor is transferred to the hands and may then reach the face or remaining PPE
The anti-fog coating on the visor is scratched, reducing visibility if the shield is worn again later
The headband stretches out of shape so the shield no longer sits securely on the wearer's head
The visor cracks along a stress point, so the shield must be discarded instead of being reprocessed

rationales.whyCorrect: CDC doffing instructions direct the wearer to handle eye protection by the headband or earpieces because the outside front of any PPE item is the surface most likely to be contaminated. Grasping the visor deposits whatever splashed onto it directly onto the hands, which are then used to remove the mask or respirator right beside the eyes, nose, and mouth — a direct self-contamination pathway from a soiled surface to a mucous membrane. The other listed consequences are equipment-durability problems, not exposure problems; this is why doffing is taught as a sequence of designated clean handholds rather than simply as taking things off.
rationales.eli10: Picture taking a hot pan out of the oven. You do not grab the pan — you grab the handle, because the handle is the part that is safe to hold. Every piece of PPE has a designated handle: for a face shield it is the headband behind your head, for goggles the earpieces, for a gown the ties, for gloves the cuff. The front of the shield is the part that caught the splashes, so touching it moves whatever landed there onto your fingers. Those fingers then travel up to your mask, right next to your eyes, nose, and mouth — exactly the trip you spent the whole encounter preventing.

questions.stem: Which comparison of a surgical mask and an N95 filtering facepiece respirator is accurate?

options.text: Both form a tight seal against the face; the N95 simply uses thicker filter material and lasts longer
A surgical mask filters smaller particles than an N95 does, but it offers no protection from fluid splash
A surgical mask is a loose-fitting droplet and splash barrier, while an N95 seals to the face and filters at least 95% of airborne particles
An N95 protects only the patient from the wearer, while a surgical mask protects only the wearer from the patient

rationales.whyCorrect: A surgical mask is a loose-fitting, fluid-resistant barrier worn over the nose and mouth; because unfiltered air passes freely around its edges, it is not designed to protect the wearer from small airborne particles. An N95 is a NIOSH-approved filtering facepiece respirator that must seal against the face and is certified to filter at least 95% of airborne particles. A common misstatement is that the N95 filters particles '0.3 micrometers and larger' — in fact NIOSH tests at roughly the most-penetrating particle size, near 0.3 micrometers, and filtration efficiency is higher for particles both larger and smaller than that, so 95% is a worst-case floor rather than a size cutoff. Because the N95's performance depends on a seal, it requires fit testing and a user seal check, while a surgical mask requires neither.
rationales.eli10: Compare a window screen to a diving mask. A window screen keeps insects and splashing rain out, and it is good at that, but air moves freely around and through it. A diving mask has to press tightly against your face, because even a small gap is where water comes in. A surgical mask is the screen: it catches droplets and splashes flying at your mouth and nose. An N95 is the diving mask: it must seal, so the air you breathe is forced through the filter material instead of slipping around the edges. That is also why only the N95 needs fit testing — a screen does not have to match your face, but a seal does.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: A surgical mask is a loose-fitting, fluid-resistant barrier worn over the nose and mouth; because unfiltered air passes freely around its edges, it is not designed to protect the wearer from small airborne particles. An N95 is a NIOSH-approved filtering facepiece respirator that must seal against the face and is certified to filter at least 95% of airborne particles. questions.stem: Which example best illustrates appropriate use of gloves during patient care?

options.text: Wearing the same gloves to care for two patients in the same room because each needs only a brief vital-sign check
Pulling a second pair of gloves over visibly soiled gloves so a dressing change can continue without interruption
Applying alcohol-based hand rub to the outside of gloved hands to decontaminate them before the next task
Removing gloves, performing hand hygiene, and donning a fresh pair between perineal care and a dressing change

rationales.whyCorrect: Gloves are changed whenever care moves from a contaminated body site to a clean body site on the same patient, and always between patients, with hand hygiene performed after removal because gloves may have unrecognized micropunctures and hands are readily contaminated during doffing. Disinfecting gloves in place is not an accepted substitute: alcohol-based product is not validated on glove material, can degrade it, and leaves organic soil on the surface. Layering a clean pair over soiled gloves likewise traps rather than removes the contamination, and it produces an unpredictable fit. Wearing one pair across two patients is not excused by the tasks being brief or identical, or by the patients sharing a room; treating a single pair of gloves as reusable across sites or patients is one of the most common PPE errors observed in practice.
rationales.eli10: Gloves work like paper towels, not like oven mitts. You use a paper towel for one mess and throw it away — you would not wipe up something soiled and then dry a clean dish with that same towel. Providing perineal care and then touching an open dressing with the same gloves carries organisms straight from the dirtiest site to the one most vulnerable to infection. Sanitizer does not rescue the situation either: it was designed and tested for skin, not for glove material, and it can weaken the glove while the soil stays sitting on the surface. New task in a cleaner spot means new gloves, and clean hands in between.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Gloves are changed whenever care moves from a contaminated body site to a clean body site on the same patient, and always between patients, with hand hygiene performed after removal because gloves may have unrecognized micropunctures and hands are readily contaminated during doffing. questions.stem: A nurse will assist with a procedure in which a substantial splash or spray of blood onto the body and face is anticipated. Which PPE selection best matches the anticipated exposure?

options.text: A fluid-resistant (impermeable) gown with a face shield worn over a mask, plus gloves
A standard non-fluid-resistant isolation gown with goggles worn over a mask, plus gloves
A cloth cover gown with a surgical mask and no eye protection, plus gloves
A fluid-resistant gown with a surgical mask and no eye protection, plus gloves

rationales.whyCorrect: PPE is selected by the anticipated route and volume of exposure, not by the patient's diagnosis. CDC guidance calls for a fluid-resistant or impermeable gown whenever soaking or penetration by blood or body fluids is likely, and for protection of the mouth, nose, and eyes whenever splashes or sprays are anticipated; a face shield worn over a mask covers the eyes while the mask underneath protects the nose and mouth. The other options each leave one anticipated route open: a standard isolation gown wets through under real fluid volume, and any selection without eye protection leaves the ocular mucous membranes exposed to the splash the nurse already expects. A cloth cover gown provides essentially no fluid barrier at all.
rationales.eli10: Choosing PPE is like dressing for a forecast. A windbreaker handles drizzle, but if the forecast says downpour you want something water cannot soak through, plus something over your face. A standard isolation gown is the windbreaker — it wets through when real fluid volume hits it. A fluid-resistant gown is the rain slicker. Your eyes, nose, and mouth are wet, open doorways for organisms, so when a splash is expected all three need covering: the face shield guards the eyes, the mask underneath guards the nose and mouth. Notice that you built this choice from what you expect to hit you, not from anything written in the patient's chart.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: PPE is selected by the anticipated route and volume of exposure, not by the patient's diagnosis. CDC guidance calls for a fluid-resistant or impermeable gown whenever soaking or penetration by blood or body fluids is likely, and for protection of the mouth, nose, and eyes whenever splashes or sprays are anticipated; a face shield worn over a mask covers the eyes while the mask underneath protects the nose and mouth. questions.stem: Which statement about eye protection as a form of PPE is accurate?

options.text: A face shield worn alone can substitute for a mask because it covers the nose and mouth as well as the eyes
Goggles worn snugly protect the mucous membranes of the eyes, nose, and mouth from splashes and sprays
Eye protection is removed first during doffing because its outer surface is the least contaminated of any PPE worn
Personal prescription eyeglasses are not adequate eye protection because they leave the sides and top exposed

rationales.whyCorrect: CDC states that personal eyeglasses and contact lenses are not considered adequate eye protection, because ordinary spectacles leave the sides, top, and bottom of the eye open to a splash arriving from any angle other than straight ahead. Goggles or a face shield must be worn instead, and goggles are manufactured in styles designed to fit over prescription glasses. Goggles cover only the eyes, however snugly they fit, so a mask is still required for the nose and mouth; a face shield alone is likewise not accepted as a substitute for a mask even though it hangs in front of the nose and mouth, because it is open at the sides and bottom and does not filter inhaled air; and in CDC's doffing sequence gloves come off first, with eye protection removed after them by the headband or earpieces because its outer surface is treated as contaminated.
rationales.eli10: Regular eyeglasses are like holding an umbrella straight out in front of you during a windy storm — rain still arrives from the sides and over the top. Goggles behave more like a helmet visor: they wrap around and close those gaps, so a splash coming in at an angle still cannot reach your eyes. Your eyes matter here because their moist surface is an entry route for organisms, just like your nose and mouth. And goggles cover only the eyes, so a mask still goes on underneath — each piece of gear does one job, and you have to cover every doorway you expect to be hit.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: CDC states that personal eyeglasses and contact lenses are not considered adequate eye protection, because ordinary spectacles leave the sides, top, and bottom of the eye open to a splash arriving from any angle other than straight ahead. Goggles or a face shield must be worn instead, and goggles are manufactured in styles designed to fit over prescription glasses. questions.stem: In the hierarchy of controls, PPE is placed at the bottom and described as the last line of defense. Which statement best explains why it is ranked there?

options.text: PPE is the most expensive control to purchase and maintain, so it is used only after cheaper options fail
PPE works against contact transmission but gives no meaningful protection against droplet or airborne exposure
PPE leaves the hazard in place and works only when it is correctly selected, correctly fitted, and used at every encounter
PPE requirements come from professional recommendations rather than from law, so employers cannot be held to them

rationales.whyCorrect: Controls higher in the hierarchy — elimination, substitution, engineering controls, and administrative controls — reduce risk whether or not any individual worker remembers to act, because they change the hazard itself or the environment around it. PPE leaves the hazard fully present and interposes a barrier that functions only if the right item is chosen for the anticipated exposure, fits the wearer, is donned and doffed without self-contamination, and is used every single time by every person exposed. That dependence on flawless, repeated human performance makes PPE the least reliable layer, not the least important one. The ranking is not about cost, and it is not about limited effectiveness against particular routes: correctly selected PPE addresses contact, droplet, and airborne exposure. PPE use is also legally enforceable in the United States under OSHA standards, so it is far more than a professional recommendation.
rationales.eli10: Compare two ways of keeping people from being hurt by a hole in a sidewalk. You could fill in the hole, and then nobody can fall in, ever, whether or not they are paying attention. Or everyone walking past could wear knee pads. The knee pads genuinely help, but the hole is still there, and they only work if every person remembers them, has the right size, and puts them on correctly, every single day. PPE is the knee pads. Ranking it last is not a claim that it is weak or optional — it is a claim about reliability: it protects one person at a time and can fail the moment someone is rushed, tired, undertrained, or handed the wrong size.

questions.stem: During a supply shortage, a facility's policy refers to both 'extended use' and 'reuse' of N95 respirators. Which comparison of these two terms is accurate?

options.text: Extended use means donning the same respirator again for a later encounter, while reuse means wearing one continuously across several encounters
Extended use means wearing a respirator past the manufacturer's printed shelf-life date, while reuse means decontaminating and redistributing respirators between staff members
Extended use means wearing the same respirator continuously across multiple encounters without removing it, while reuse means removing the respirator and donning that same one again later
Both terms describe layering a surgical mask over an N95 so that a single respirator can serve for an entire shift

rationales.whyCorrect: CDC and NIOSH define extended use as wearing the same N95 continuously for encounters with several patients without removing it between them, and limited reuse as taking the respirator off after an encounter and putting that same respirator back on for a later one. Extended use is generally favored over reuse because each doffing and re-donning cycle adds an opportunity to contaminate the hands from the respirator's contaminated outer surface and to disturb the facepiece seal. Neither is routine practice: on CDC/NIOSH's surge-capacity tiers, extended use is a contingency capacity strategy while limited reuse is a crisis capacity strategy, which is consistent with extended use being the preferred of the two. Neither term refers to sharing a respirator between individuals: a filtering facepiece respirator is reused only by the same wearer, because fit is established for one specific person's face.
rationales.eli10: Picture a pair of muddy boots. Extended use is keeping them on the whole time you move between four different garden beds — your hands never touch the muddy outside. Reuse is pulling them off between each bed and tugging them back on again, and every one of those cycles puts your fingers on the dirty part and shifts how they sit. That is exactly why extended use is usually the safer of the two: fewer chances to touch a contaminated surface, and fewer chances to disturb the seal. Neither one is the everyday plan — hospitals reach for extended use first when supplies get tight, and only fall back on reuse when they get much tighter. And one rule never bends: a respirator is fitted to one specific face, so it is never passed to a coworker, no matter how short supplies get.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between Transmission-Based Precautions and Standard Precautions?

options.text: Transmission-Based Precautions replace Standard Precautions once a specific pathogen has been identified
Standard Precautions apply to confirmed infections, while Transmission-Based Precautions apply to suspected ones
Transmission-Based Precautions are layered on top of Standard Precautions when a pathogen's route of spread demands added measures
Standard Precautions are used in ambulatory settings, while Transmission-Based Precautions are used in inpatient settings

rationales.whyCorrect: CDC guidance states that Transmission-Based Precautions are used in addition to Standard Precautions, never instead of them. Standard Precautions are the baseline applied to every patient in every setting regardless of diagnosis or suspected infection status; Transmission-Based Precautions add route-specific barriers, room placement, and transport rules for patients known or suspected to carry agents spread by contact, droplet, or airborne routes. Treating the two as a substitution is a serious conceptual error, since baseline protections against blood and body-fluid exposure remain necessary at all times, and the setting of care does not determine which system applies.
rationales.eli10: Standard Precautions are the seatbelt you buckle every single time you get in a car, no exceptions, no matter who is driving. Transmission-Based Precautions are the extra gear you add when the trip is riskier: a helmet, pads, a roll cage. Nobody unbuckles the seatbelt in order to put the helmet on. That is what 'in addition to' means in CDC's wording, and it is why identifying a pathogen never lets you drop the baseline.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: CDC guidance states that Transmission-Based Precautions are used in addition to Standard Precautions, never instead of them. questions.stem: Which grouping correctly names the three categories of Transmission-Based Precautions defined by the CDC?

options.text: Contact, Droplet, Airborne
Contact, Droplet, Bloodborne
Contact, Respiratory, Airborne
Droplet, Airborne, Protective Environment

rationales.whyCorrect: CDC recognizes exactly three Transmission-Based Precaution categories — Contact, Droplet, and Airborne — each named for the principal route by which an infectious agent moves from a source to a susceptible host. The distractors borrow real but different concepts: bloodborne exposure is managed under Standard Precautions rather than a separate isolation category; 'respiratory' is a descriptive adjective, not a CDC category; and a Protective Environment is a specialized positive-pressure room for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients, which shields a vulnerable patient rather than containing a pathogen and is therefore not a Transmission-Based Precaution.
rationales.eli10: Ask how a germ gets a ride to the next person. Some hitchhike on hands, bed rails, and doorknobs, which is Contact. Some ride heavy spit-drops that arc out of a cough and land within a few feet, which is Droplet. Some float like campfire smoke and drift far from where they started, which is Airborne. The categories are named after the ride, not after the germ or the body system it attacks, so once you know how something travels you already know its category.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: CDC recognizes exactly three Transmission-Based Precaution categories — Contact, Droplet, and Airborne — each named for the principal route by which an infectious agent moves from a source to a susceptible host. questions.stem: What personal protective equipment does CDC guidance specify for routine entry into the space of a patient on Contact Precautions?

options.text: Gloves alone, with a gown added only when visible soiling is anticipated
A surgical mask and gloves, donned at the doorway before entry
A fit-tested N95 respirator and gloves, donned before entry
A gown and gloves, donned before entering the patient's space

rationales.whyCorrect: Contact Precautions call for gown and gloves for all interactions that may involve contact with the patient or with potentially contaminated surfaces in the patient's environment. CDC specifies donning on room entry and removal before exit so that contamination stays contained within the patient's space. Waiting until soiling seems likely defeats the purpose, because surfaces near the patient are already presumed contaminated whether or not soiling is visible. Masks and respirators are the defining PPE of Droplet and Airborne Precautions respectively, not Contact Precautions.
rationales.eli10: Contact germs travel by touch, so you cover the two things that do the touching: your hands and your clothes. Gloves handle the hands, and a gown handles the front of your uniform, which brushes the bed rail, the mattress, and the IV pole without you noticing. It is like painting a room: you put on the gloves and old clothes before you start, not after paint is already on your sleeve. And you take them off inside the room so the paint does not ride into the hallway with you.

questions.stem: Why do Airborne Precautions require a fit-tested N95 or higher-level respirator, while Droplet Precautions call only for a surgical mask?

options.text: Surgical masks filter more efficiently than respirators but cannot be tolerated for the long shifts that airborne isolation requires
Organisms spread by droplets are inherently less virulent, so a lower level of respiratory protection is considered acceptable for them
Airborne agents spread mainly by contaminated surfaces, and a respirator mainly keeps personnel from touching their own faces
Airborne agents ride particles small enough to stay suspended and drift from the source, while droplets fall out of the air within a few feet

rationales.whyCorrect: The distinction rests on particle behavior, not on how dangerous the organism is. Droplet nuclei carrying airborne agents remain suspended on air currents and can be inhaled at a distance and over time, so protection requires a device that both filters small particles efficiently and seals to the wearer's face — which is why respirators must be fit tested and why a loose surgical mask is inadequate. Larger respiratory droplets travel only short distances before settling, so a surgical mask worn during close contact intercepts them. Virulence, surface contamination, and wearer tolerance do not drive the requirement.
rationales.eli10: Picture two different sprays. A garden hose throws heavy drops that arc out and hit the ground a few feet away, and a shield held in front of you blocks those. That shield is the surgical mask. Now picture campfire smoke: it drifts, curls around corners, and slips through any gap, so a shield with loose edges is useless. You need something that seals tight to your face and filters the tiny bits, and someone has to verify the seal on your particular face. That verification is fit testing.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the pressure and air-handling requirements of an airborne infection isolation room (AIIR)?

options.text: To draw air in from surrounding areas and exhaust it outdoors or through a HEPA filter before recirculation
To exchange air fast enough that respiratory protection may be removed once the door has stayed closed
To hold the room above corridor pressure so airborne contaminants from the unit cannot reach the patient
To vent room air into the corridor return duct so the unit's general ventilation can dilute it

rationales.whyCorrect: An AIIR is engineered with monitored negative pressure relative to surrounding areas, a minimum of 12 air changes per hour in new construction or renovation and 6 per hour in existing facilities, and exhaust either directly outdoors or through HEPA filtration before any recirculation. Air therefore moves from the corridor into the room and never the reverse, and whatever leaves is diluted and filtered. This is an engineering control protecting people outside the room; the air inside remains contaminated, so it never substitutes for respirator use. A room held above corridor pressure describes a Protective Environment, which serves the opposite purpose.
rationales.eli10: A negative-pressure room is a room that inhales. Air slides in from the hallway under the door and never sneaks back out, and the air pulled from the room is blown outside the building or run through a HEPA filter that traps the particles. Think of a range hood that pulls smoke straight out instead of letting it wander through the house. Notice who this protects: everyone outside. Inside, the air is still smoky, which is exactly why the respirator stays on.

questions.stem: Which comparison of Contact and Droplet Precautions is accurate?

options.text: Contact Precautions permit an open bay with no spatial separation, while Droplet Precautions always require a single-patient room with the door closed
Contact Precautions target spread by touching the patient or nearby surfaces, while Droplet Precautions target short-range respiratory spread
Contact Precautions require a surgical mask on room entry, while Droplet Precautions require a gown and gloves for each patient contact
Droplet Precautions require a fit-tested N95 respirator, while Contact Precautions require a mask worn within three feet of the patient

rationales.whyCorrect: Each category is built around a specific transmission route, and the required barrier follows from that route. Contact Precautions interrupt direct and indirect contact transmission using gown and gloves plus dedicated patient-care equipment; Droplet Precautions interrupt short-range respiratory spread using a mask donned on room entry. Choice C simply swaps those barriers. A fit-tested N95 respirator and a negative-pressure AIIR belong to Airborne Precautions, not Droplet, so choice D is wrong. Both categories prefer a single-patient room, and when one is unavailable CDC advises at least 3 feet of spatial separation with the privacy curtain drawn, so an open bay without separation is unacceptable for Contact and a closed door is not mandated for Droplet, ruling out choice A.
rationales.eli10: Match the barrier to the vehicle. Droplet germs move like sneeze-spray that arcs out and lands within a few feet, so you put a barrier in front of your face and keep some distance. If you catch yourself memorizing which gear goes with which disease, back up and ask how the germ is traveling; the gear follows from that.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if a room being used for Airborne Precautions were mistakenly set to positive pressure relative to the corridor?

options.text: Air carrying infectious particles would be pushed out of the room into the corridor, especially when the door opened
Airflow direction would reverse, but the required air changes per hour would still prevent particles from escaping
Little would change for others on the unit, as long as staff wore fit-tested respirators while inside the room
Infectious particles would be held inside the room by the higher pressure, improving containment

rationales.whyCorrect: The pressure differential determines the direction of airflow across the doorway. questions.stem: Which example correctly pairs a condition with the Transmission-Based Precaution category CDC guidance assigns to it?

options.text: Seasonal influenza — Airborne Precautions with placement in an AIIR
Pulmonary tuberculosis — Airborne Precautions with placement in an AIIR
Norovirus gastroenteritis — Droplet Precautions with a surgical mask worn on entry
Pertussis (whooping cough) — Contact Precautions with gown and gloves on entry

rationales.whyCorrect: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is carried on droplet nuclei that remain suspended in air, placing it with measles and varicella in the Airborne category requiring an AIIR and respiratory protection. Influenza and Bordetella pertussis spread through larger respiratory droplets over short distances and are managed with Droplet Precautions, with pertussis continued until five days of effective antimicrobial therapy are complete. Norovirus spreads by the fecal-oral route through contaminated hands and surfaces and requires Contact Precautions, which CDC continues for a minimum of 48 hours after symptoms resolve.
rationales.eli10: Sort by how each germ gets around and the pairings settle themselves. TB rides tiny particles that hang in the air like smoke, so Airborne. Flu and whooping cough ride bigger cough-drops that fall within a few feet, so Droplet. Norovirus rides hands and surfaces touched after vomiting or diarrhea, so Contact. Each wrong pairing here is a barrier aimed at a route the germ does not actually use, which is precisely how an outbreak gets started while everyone believes they are protected.

questions.stem: A patient on Airborne Precautions for pulmonary tuberculosis requires a medically necessary imaging study outside the unit. Which action best reflects CDC transport guidance?

options.text: Postpone the study until sputum smears are negative, since transport is prohibited while the patient is infectious
Place a fit-tested N95 respirator on the patient and have the transporting staff member wear a surgical mask
Place a surgical mask on the patient and require every staff member along the transport route to don a fit-tested respirator
Place a surgical mask on the patient; the transporting staff member need not wear a respirator while the patient remains masked

rationales.whyCorrect: CDC directs facilities to limit transport of patients on Airborne Precautions to medically necessary purposes and, when transport is required, to have the patient wear a surgical mask and observe respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette. Because the mask provides source control at the point of generation, CDC states that personnel transporting the patient do not need to wear a mask or respirator if the patient is masked and any infectious skin lesions are covered. Masking the patient with an N95 is not recommended, since respirators are designed to protect a wearer from inhaled hazards and increase breathing effort for an ill patient. Medically necessary studies are not prohibited.
rationales.eli10: There are two places to stop a problem: at the source, or at every person downstream. Masking the patient stops it at the source, like putting a lid on a pot so steam never fills the kitchen, instead of handing everyone in the house an umbrella. That is source control, and it is why the corridor full of staff does not need respirators. The mask on the patient is an ordinary surgical mask, because its job is catching what comes out, not filtering what goes in.

questions.stem: Which action is specific to Contact Precautions for Clostridioides difficile infection, rather than a feature of Contact Precautions generally?

options.text: Wearing a gown and gloves for all contact with the patient and the patient's immediate environment
Using soap and water for hand hygiene and an EPA List K sporicidal agent for room cleaning, because spores resist alcohol
Placing the patient in a single-patient room with dedicated patient-care equipment
Limiting the patient's transport outside the room to purposes that are medically necessary

rationales.whyCorrect: Gown and gloves, single-room placement, dedicated equipment, and limiting transport are elements of Contact Precautions for any organism; a private bathroom is not a separate requirement, since it follows automatically whenever any Contact Precautions patient is placed in a single-patient room. What distinguishes C. difficile is spore formation: spores are not reliably inactivated by alcohol-based hand rub or by many routine disinfectants, so CDC recommends handwashing with soap and water, which physically removes spores, and cleaning with an EPA-registered sporicidal product from List K. CDC's Appendix A lists the duration of Contact Precautions as the duration of illness; the more conservative practice of continuing at least 48 hours after diarrhea resolves comes from SHEA/IDSA guidance and from facility policy, not from CDC's isolation guideline.
rationales.eli10: C. difficile can wrap itself in a hard shell and become a spore, essentially an armored seed that shrugs off what kills ordinary bacteria. Alcohol gel cannot crack that shell, but soap and running water physically scrub the spores loose and rinse them away, which is removal rather than killing. The same logic applies to the room: an ordinary wipe leaves spores on the bed rail, so a bleach-type sporicidal cleaner is needed. Everything else on this list is routine Contact Precautions; the spore-specific steps are the C. diff signature.

questions.stem: A patient presents with several weeks of cough, fever, night sweats, and weight loss, and sputum testing is pending. Which principle best guides the choice of precautions at this point?

options.text: Precautions should await a laboratory-confirmed diagnosis, since isolating patients who prove uninfected wastes limited resources
Standard Precautions alone are adequate until a specific organism has been identified by the laboratory
Airborne Precautions in an AIIR should begin now based on the syndrome, and be discontinued if tuberculosis is excluded
Contact Precautions should be applied empirically, since gown and gloves cover the widest range of unknown organisms

rationales.whyCorrect: CDC directs that Transmission-Based Precautions be applied empirically, based on the clinical syndrome and the likely etiologic agents, while diagnostic confirmation is pending. CDC's table of syndromes warranting empiric precautions assigns Airborne Precautions to cough, fever, and pulmonary infiltrate consistent with tuberculosis. Mycobacterial diagnostics take days for nucleic acid amplification and serial smears and weeks for culture, so every hour of delay is unprotected exposure for staff, visitors, and other patients. Precautions are readily discontinued once the diagnosis is excluded, making the asymmetry of harms strongly favor acting first.
rationales.eli10: Nobody waits for the fire department to confirm a real fire before leaving the building; the alarm is enough to act on. A cluster of symptoms is that alarm. Act and be wrong, and the cost is a few days in a special room for one patient. Wait and be right, and everyone who walked past that doorway was breathing unprotected the whole time. Start on the syndrome, then stop when the test clears the patient. Contact Precautions would be the wrong alarm entirely, since gown and gloves do nothing about air.

questions.stem: A patient is admitted with disseminated varicella (chickenpox). Which set of precautions is indicated, and on what reasoning?

options.text: Airborne Precautions alone, because an AIIR contains the virus and gown and gloves add nothing meaningful
Droplet plus Contact Precautions, because respiratory secretions and skin lesions both transmit only at close range
Airborne plus Contact Precautions, because the virus spreads on small airborne particles and in vesicle fluid
Contact Precautions alone, because the skin lesions are the only source of infectious virus in chickenpox

rationales.whyCorrect: Some pathogens travel by more than one route, and precautions are combined accordingly. Varicella-zoster virus is disseminated in small particles capable of airborne spread and is also present in high concentration in vesicle fluid, so CDC's Appendix A pairs Airborne Precautions in an AIIR with Contact Precautions using gown and gloves, continued for the duration of illness. An AIIR addresses only the airborne route and leaves direct contact with lesion fluid unaddressed. CDC further advises that susceptible, non-immune healthcare personnel not enter the room when immune caregivers are available, an administrative control layered on top of the barriers.
rationales.eli10: Chickenpox has two travel routes: it drifts through the air from the airway, and it sits in the fluid inside every blister, ready to move on hands and sleeves. Two roads in means two roadblocks, so the respirator and negative-pressure room close the air route while gown and gloves close the touch route. Closing only one is locking the front door and leaving the back door open. Whenever a pathogen has more than one route, you stack the categories rather than picking the scarier-sounding one.

questions.stem: Which term refers to the habitat where an infectious agent normally lives, grows, and multiplies before it can reach a new host?

options.text: Portal of exit
Reservoir
Vehicle
Susceptible host

rationales.whyCorrect: CDC's epidemiology framework defines the reservoir as the habitat in which an agent normally lives, grows, and multiplies; reservoirs may be human, animal, or environmental. This is distinct from the portal of exit, which is the anatomic route the agent uses to leave that habitat, and from a vehicle, which is an inanimate intermediary that merely carries an agent between people without supporting its growth. Identifying the reservoir matters clinically because interventions aimed at this link (treating or decolonizing infected people, excluding ill personnel, eliminating stagnant water in respiratory equipment) remove the source itself rather than blocking one of its routes.
rationales.eli10: A reservoir is where a germ lives full time: its address, not its exit door and not its ride. There are three kinds of addresses: people (an infected wound, bacteria carried in someone's nose), animals (a bat, a rodent, a farm animal), and the environment (soil, standing water in a humidifier reservoir). The test is whether the organism can actually grow and reproduce there. A bed rail that got contaminated an hour ago usually fails that test, so it is a surface a germ was dropped onto, not a home. The distinction changes your action: you treat or remove a reservoir, but you clean a surface.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central principle behind the phrase "breaking the chain of infection"?

options.text: All six links must be eliminated at the same time for transmission to stop.
The infectious agent is the only link that can realistically be interrupted.
The model applies only to infections that spread through the air.
Interrupting any single link is enough to stop transmission to a new host.

rationales.whyCorrect: The chain of infection is a model of sequential dependencies: the agent must leave a reservoir, travel by some route, enter a new host, and find that host susceptible, with each step conditional on the one before it. Because of that dependency, removing or neutralizing any one link ends that transmission event, which is why prevention programs have many effective options rather than one. The model describes contact, droplet, and airborne spread equally, and links other than the agent (the reservoir, the routes, host immunity) are usually the most controllable in practice.
rationales.eli10: Each step in the chain only happens if the previous one did. A germ that never leaves its reservoir cannot ride anywhere; one that rides but finds no way in cannot infect. So you do not have to defeat the organism at every step, you only need one step to fail. That is why a unit can attack whichever link it controls best: cleaning shared equipment and hand hygiene attack the ride, tissues and masks attack the exit, vaccination attacks susceptibility. Any one of those, done reliably, ends that particular transmission.

questions.stem: Which sequence lists the links of the chain of infection in the order a pathogen actually travels?

options.text: Infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host
Infectious agent, portal of entry, reservoir, mode of transmission, portal of exit, susceptible host
Susceptible host, reservoir, infectious agent, portal of exit, portal of entry, mode of transmission
Reservoir, infectious agent, portal of entry, mode of transmission, portal of exit, susceptible host

rationales.whyCorrect: The standard model begins with an infectious agent that lives in a reservoir, leaves through a portal of exit, travels by a mode of transmission, enters a new person through a portal of entry, and finally must encounter a host who is susceptible. questions.stem: Which comparison between direct and indirect transmission is accurate?

options.text: Direct transmission occurs only in community settings such as homes and schools, while indirect transmission occurs only inside healthcare facilities.
Direct transmission applies only to bloodborne agents such as HIV, while indirect transmission applies only to respiratory agents such as influenza.
Direct transmission moves the agent from source to host with nothing in between, while indirect transmission uses an object, the air, or a vector.
Direct transmission requires a host whose defenses are already breached, while indirect transmission can infect a person with fully intact defenses.

rationales.whyCorrect: Direct transmission means the agent moves from source to host with nothing in between, through skin or mucous membrane contact or droplet spray traveling a short distance. CDC defines indirect transmission as transfer from reservoir to host by suspended air particles, inanimate objects (vehicles), or animate intermediaries (vectors), so the defining feature is the presence of an intermediary. Both routes still require and terminate in a susceptible host (D), both occur inside and outside healthcare settings (A), and neither is restricted to a single class of pathogen (B).
rationales.eli10: One question separates the two: did anything carry the germ in between? If a person hands it to a person, by touch or by a cough landing on someone at close range, that is direct. If a doorknob, a shared cup, a droplet nucleus drifting across a room, or a mosquito did the carrying, that is indirect. Notice what the split is not about. It is not about which organism, not about hospital versus community, and it does not let the receiving person off the hook. Either route still ends at someone whose defenses can be breached.

questions.stem: A client with influenza is taught to cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue. Which link is this action designed to interrupt, and why?

options.text: Reservoir, because the tissue removes the virus from the client's respiratory tract
Portal of exit, because it blocks the route the virus uses to leave the infected host
Susceptible host, because the tissue raises the client's own resistance to the virus
Portal of entry, because it seals the mucous membranes the virus would use to get in

rationales.whyCorrect: Respiratory secretions expelled from the nose and mouth are influenza's portal of exit, so containing them at the source interrupts the chain at that specific link. The tissue does not eliminate virus already replicating in the respiratory epithelium, so the client remains a reservoir, and it does nothing to alter the client's immune status. Source control is emphasized in respiratory hygiene programs precisely because blocking exit protects every potential contact at once, before the agent ever enters a transmission route.
rationales.eli10: The portal of exit is the doorway an organism uses to get out of the body it is currently in, and for respiratory viruses that doorway is the nose and mouth. A tissue cures nothing: the virus is still multiplying in the airway, so the reservoir is untouched, and the person's immunity is unchanged. What the tissue does is catch secretions at the instant they leave. Blocking exit is efficient because one action protects everyone downstream at the same time, which is why source control is a first move in respiratory outbreaks.

questions.stem: An infectious agent leaves its reservoir and reaches a new person, but that person's skin is unbroken and no mucous membrane contact occurs. What is the most likely outcome, and why?

options.text: Infection would still occur, because exposure to a pathogen is by itself enough to establish infection.
The chain would be broken at the mode of transmission, because the agent never actually reached a host.
Infection would not occur, because the chain is interrupted at the portal of entry.
Infection would be delayed rather than prevented, because intact skin only slows microbial invasion.

rationales.whyCorrect: CDC defines the portal of entry as the route that must provide the pathogen access to tissues in which it can multiply, and intact skin is a first-line nonspecific defense that denies that access. Without a break in the skin, mucous membrane contact, or a device that tunnels past the barrier, the entry link fails and the chain stops, so exposure alone does not equal infection. The agent did reach the person, so the mode-of-transmission link succeeded; this is the rationale behind maintaining skin integrity, using aseptic technique, and limiting invasive device days.
rationales.eli10: Arriving is not the same as invading. The definition of a portal of entry requires access to tissue where the organism can multiply, and unbroken skin does not provide that. No cut, no mucous membrane contact, no line or catheter tunneling under the barrier, and the chain simply ends there. One caution keeps this from being falsely reassuring: organisms sitting on intact skin are not harmless, because hands carry them onward to eyes, noses, and wounds, which are real entry points. The barrier holds only as long as the germ stays where it landed.

questions.stem: Which example illustrates vector-borne transmission rather than transmission by a vehicle?

options.text: A shared blood pressure cuff carries bacteria from one client to the next.
A mosquito bite passes a bloodborne parasite from an infected person to a new host.
Improperly refrigerated food transmits Salmonella to guests at a catered event.
Contaminated drinking water spreads an intestinal pathogen through a community.

rationales.whyCorrect: A vector is a living intermediary, typically an arthropod such as a mosquito, tick, or flea, that carries an agent to a new host either mechanically on its body or after the agent develops within it. A vehicle is an inanimate intermediary such as water, food, equipment, or another fomite. Both are subtypes of indirect transmission, but the distinction drives practice: cleaning and disinfection address vehicles, whereas vector control depends on habitat reduction, repellents, and physical barriers.
rationales.eli10: Vectors and vehicles are both middlemen for germs, and the sorting rule is simply alive or not alive. Water, food, a shared cuff, a bed rail: inanimate, so vehicle. A mosquito, tick, or flea is alive and seeks out hosts on its own, so vector. Some vectors are only couriers carrying the organism on their bodies, while in others the organism actually develops inside the insect before it can be transmitted. The reason the split matters is that the countermeasures share nothing: you can disinfect a vehicle, but you cannot disinfect a mosquito.

questions.stem: After using a shared point-of-care blood glucose meter on one client, a nurse cleans and disinfects the device with an EPA-registered product before taking it to the next client. Which link of the chain does this practice target?

options.text: Reservoir, because the meter is the habitat in which these organisms normally live and multiply
Portal of exit, because disinfection prevents organisms from leaving the first client's bloodstream
Mode of transmission, because the contaminated meter would otherwise act as a vehicle carrying organisms to the next client
Portal of entry, because disinfection closes the fingerstick puncture site used to obtain the sample

rationales.whyCorrect: A device contaminated during use on one person and then carried to another is functioning as an inanimate vehicle, which places it squarely in the mode-of-transmission link; cleaning and disinfecting between clients removes that route. The meter is not a reservoir, because organisms are deposited on it rather than living and multiplying there, and disinfection changes neither the first client's exit route nor the next client's puncture site. Shared blood glucose meters are a well-documented source of hepatitis B transmission, which is why CDC advises assigning them to a single person whenever possible and cleaning and disinfecting them after every use when sharing is unavoidable.
rationales.eli10: Equipment that moves between people is one of the most reliable rides a germ ever gets, and rides belong to the mode-of-transmission link. Check what disinfecting actually changes: the first client is still colonized or infected, so the reservoir is intact; that client's exit routes are unchanged; and the next client still has a fingertip that will be punctured, so the entry point is unchanged. The only thing you eliminated was the vehicle. Glucose meters are the classic example because they touch blood and travel from room to room.

questions.stem: Which facility-wide change would most directly break the chain of infection at the susceptible-host link?

options.text: Offering seasonal influenza vaccination to clients, staff, and volunteers
Requiring covered, leak-proof transport containers for used instruments
Adopting a standardized terminal cleaning protocol for discharge rooms
Posting respiratory etiquette signs and tissue stations at all entrances

rationales.whyCorrect: Vaccination produces specific acquired immunity, converting a potentially susceptible person into one whose defenses can neutralize the agent, which is by definition action on the susceptible-host link; CDC recommends annual influenza vaccination for everyone 6 months and older, including health care personnel. Terminal cleaning and covered instrument transport act on the mode of transmission by removing or containing vehicles, and respiratory etiquette acts on the portal of exit. Mapping each program element to its link is what lets a team see where its efforts are redundant and where a link is left unguarded.
rationales.eli10: Nearly all infection prevention works by keeping the organism away from the person. Vaccination is the exception: it allows the encounter to happen and changes the result. By presenting the immune system with a harmless preview, it builds antibodies and memory cells in advance, so an arriving pathogen is much more likely to be neutralized quickly, and illness that happens anyway is usually milder. Seasonal flu vaccine lowers the odds rather than removing them, which is why vaccinated staff still perform hand hygiene and stay home when ill. Shifting those odds is exactly what the susceptible-host link means, because susceptibility is a property of the person rather than of the germ's route. Anything that raises host defenses, such as vaccines, correcting malnutrition, or controlling blood glucose, belongs to this link.

questions.stem: A nasal culture from a healthy nurse grows methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, but she has no signs or symptoms of illness. In chain-of-infection terms, how is she best described?

options.text: A susceptible host, because the organism is present on her mucous membranes
A vehicle, because she can carry the organism to clients without becoming ill herself
A portal of exit, because her nares are the structure the organism would leave through
A reservoir, because the organism lives and multiplies in her without producing disease

rationales.whyCorrect: Colonization means an organism is present and multiplying without producing signs of infection, which fits the definition of a human reservoir, or carrier: a person without apparent disease who can nonetheless transmit the agent. Her anterior nares are the portal of exit, but the person harboring the organism is the reservoir itself, and a vehicle by definition is inanimate. The distinction is clinically important because colonized people who feel entirely well are a documented source of health care-associated transmission.
rationales.eli10: Colonized and infected are different states. Since a reservoir is defined by where an organism lives and multiplies, a colonized person is a reservoir, regardless of how well she feels. Her nostrils are the exit door of that reservoir, not the reservoir itself, and calling a person a vehicle is wrong because vehicles are inanimate. This is why routine practices do not depend on already knowing who is infected.

questions.stem: During a norovirus outbreak on a long-term care unit, a review identifies staff working while having diarrhea, shared equipment cleaned only at shift end, and residents sharing a communal bathroom. Which action interrupts the chain specifically at the reservoir link?

options.text: Excluding symptomatic staff from work until published return-to-work criteria are met
Assigning symptomatic residents to a dedicated toilet that is cleaned separately and more frequently
Reinforcing hand hygiene by staff immediately after glove removal and before leaving each room
Disinfecting shared equipment with an EPA-registered agent effective against norovirus between every resident

rationales.whyCorrect: Symptomatic staff are actively shedding virus and function as human reservoirs on the unit, so removing them from the setting eliminates a source rather than merely blocking a route; CDC's norovirus outbreak guidance specifies excluding ill personnel for a minimum of 48 hours after symptoms resolve, because shedding continues after a person feels better. Equipment disinfection and hand hygiene interrupt the mode of transmission, and note that many routine disinfectants are inadequate here, so an EPA-registered product with a norovirus claim is required. Dedicating a toilet limits environmental contamination generated at the portal of exit but leaves the shedding residents in place, so it does not remove the reservoir.
rationales.eli10: When a unit is saturated with a pathogen, ask which measure removes the supply and which ones only intercept it in transit. Hand hygiene and equipment disinfection intercept, and both are worth doing, but virus keeps being produced as long as someone on the unit is shedding it. A person with active vomiting and diarrhea is producing enormous quantities of norovirus, so removing that person from the setting removes the reservoir itself. The 48-hour rule after symptoms stop exists because shedding outlasts symptoms, which is why feeling better is not the criterion for returning.

questions.stem: Removing an indwelling urinary catheter as soon as it is no longer clinically needed is among the most effective ways to reduce catheter-associated urinary tract infection. Which explanation best accounts for its effect on the chain of infection?

options.text: It eliminates the client's normal urethral flora, so no organisms remain that could ascend into the bladder.
It reduces the virulence of the organisms colonizing the periurethral area, so fewer of them are capable of invading.
It converts the client from a susceptible host into a host with lasting acquired immunity to urinary pathogens.
It removes an artificial portal of entry into the bladder and eliminates a biofilm-coated surface that acts as a reservoir.

rationales.whyCorrect: An indwelling catheter bypasses urethral defenses and the flushing action of voiding, creating a direct portal of entry by which organisms ascend either along the outside of the tube or through its lumen from a contaminated drainage system. Its surface also supports biofilm, a matrix in which organisms live and multiply while shielded from antimicrobials and host defenses, so the device itself functions as a reservoir. Removal therefore breaks two links at once, and because risk accumulates with each catheter day, CDC and AHRQ prevention programs target appropriate indications and prompt removal rather than better cleaning of the device.
rationales.eli10: A urinary catheter is two things at once: a road and a residence. It is a road because organisms can travel up the outside of the tube along the urethra, or up the inside from a contaminated drainage bag, reaching a bladder that the urethra and normal voiding usually protect. It is a residence because within days the plastic becomes coated in biofilm, a slime layer where organisms grow while shielded from antibiotics and immune cells. You cannot scrub biofilm out of a tube that is inside someone, so the intervention that actually works is time: fewer catheter days, and no catheter placed without a real indication.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines a "fall" as the term is used in patient safety reporting?

options.text: An unplanned descent to the floor or another lower surface, with or without injury, including assisted falls
A loss of balance that the person corrects independently before reaching a lower surface
A stumble into furniture or a wall during ambulation in which the person remains upright
A descent to the floor that results in a documented injury requiring medical treatment

rationales.whyCorrect: Standard reporting definitions used in AHRQ's hospital fall-prevention toolkit and in national nursing-quality benchmarking define a fall as an unplanned descent to the floor or other lower surface regardless of injury, and they explicitly count assisted falls in which staff ease a patient down. Restricting the definition to injurious events (option D) would exclude the large majority of falls and make a unit's rate look artificially low, while corrected stumbles and near-misses are tracked separately because no descent occurred. Uniform definitions are what allow fall rates to be compared across units, hospitals, and time periods.
rationales.eli10: A fall is defined by where the person ends up, not by how badly it turned out. If someone reaches the floor when they did not mean to, it counts, even if a nurse had hold of them the whole way down and even if nothing hurts afterward. That may seem like over-counting, but it is the point: the harmless landings and the broken hips come from the same underlying problem, and the harmless ones are far more common, so they are the early signal. If you only counted injuries, you would be waiting for someone to get hurt before you could see the pattern.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of universal fall precautions?

options.text: To substitute a single standardized checklist for individualized fall-risk assessment on every unit
To document that fall-prevention measures were offered before any fall event occurs
To concentrate limited staffing and equipment on the patients who score in the high-risk range
To apply basic environmental and communication safety measures to every patient, regardless of risk score

rationales.whyCorrect: Universal fall precautions in AHRQ's hospital toolkit are the measures applied to every patient: orienting the person to the room, keeping the call light and personal items within reach, keeping the bed low with brakes locked, providing nonslip footwear, and keeping floors dry, uncluttered, and adequately lit. They are called universal because acute illness, new medications, tethering equipment, and unfamiliar surroundings raise risk for essentially every hospitalized adult, including those who score low. They establish a baseline underneath individualized, risk-factor-specific interventions rather than replacing them.
rationales.eli10: Universal precautions answer a simple question: what should be true in every room, for every patient, before anyone even looks at a risk score? Bed low, brakes on, call light within arm's reach, path to the bathroom clear and lit, shoes that grip. These are cheap, they inconvenience no one, and they help the patient whose score was low but whose blood pressure drops on the third day of a new medication. Screening is imperfect, so the baseline exists to catch the people screening misses. Patients who do screen high then get extra, specific help layered on top.

questions.stem: Which example represents an extrinsic (environmental) fall risk factor rather than an intrinsic one?

options.text: Lower-extremity muscle weakness that developed during prolonged bed rest
A drop in blood pressure that occurs when the person stands up
Reduced visual acuity caused by untreated cataracts
A dimly lit hallway with equipment cords crossing the walking path

rationales.whyCorrect: Intrinsic risk factors originate within the person, including muscle weakness, orthostatic hypotension, sensory loss, cognitive impairment, incontinence, and medication effects. Extrinsic factors originate in the surroundings, including lighting, clutter, wet or uneven floors, footwear, unfamiliar room layout, and equipment or cord placement. The distinction is practical rather than academic: intrinsic factors are addressed clinically through exercise, therapy, vision correction, and medication review, while extrinsic factors are corrected by changing the environment, and most real falls arise where an intrinsic vulnerability meets an extrinsic hazard.
rationales.eli10: Sort every risk by whether it travels with the person or stays behind in the room. Weak legs, wobbly blood pressure, and cloudy vision go wherever the patient goes, so they are intrinsic. A dark hallway with cords across it stays put, so it is extrinsic. The sorting matters because it tells you who fixes the problem and how fast: an environmental hazard can be gone in two minutes with a light switch and a cord cover, while weak legs take weeks of therapy. And notice that neither one alone usually causes the fall. Strong legs handle a dark hallway; weak legs in a clear, lit room usually manage too. It is the combination that puts people down.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains why sedative-hypnotics and other psychoactive medications are classified as fall-risk-increasing drugs?

options.text: They constrict peripheral vessels, reducing protective sensation in the feet and ankles
They accelerate bone turnover, so any stumble is more likely to produce a fracture
They blunt alertness and slow the postural reactions needed to recover from a loss of balance
They stimulate the vestibular system, producing exaggerated and overly rapid balance corrections

rationales.whyCorrect: Upright stance depends on rapid, largely automatic postural responses generated from vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive input; when balance is disturbed, a corrective step or grab must occur within a fraction of a second. Central nervous system depressants such as benzodiazepines, non-benzodiazepine hypnotics, opioids, antipsychotics, and sedating antidepressants slow that processing and add drowsiness, delayed reaction time, and sometimes confusion, so the recovery response arrives too late. This is why CDC STEADI includes review of fall-risk-increasing drugs, with the goal of stopping, switching, or reducing doses where clinically feasible.
rationales.eli10: When your foot catches on something, you do not decide to catch yourself; a reflex fires and your other leg swings out before you have consciously registered the trip. That reflex is fast, and its speed is the whole margin of safety. Sedating medications turn down the speed of the nervous system, so the same reflex still happens but arrives a beat late, and a beat late is a landing instead of a save. The medication does not push anyone over. It removes the automatic rescue that normally follows the push, which is why the fix is often lowering the dose or switching drugs rather than adding equipment.

questions.stem: A fall-risk assessment includes measuring blood pressure while the patient is lying down and again after standing. What is the reason for this step?

options.text: To identify hypertension severe enough to cause a stroke during ambulation
To determine whether dehydration is severe enough to require intravenous fluid replacement
To detect orthostatic hypotension, in which pressure falls on standing and briefly reduces cerebral perfusion
To confirm that the antihypertensive regimen is producing an adequate resting pressure

rationales.whyCorrect: On standing, gravity shifts blood volume into the legs and abdomen, and baroreceptor reflexes normally restore cardiac output and pressure within seconds. When that compensation is impaired by volume depletion, antihypertensives or other vasoactive drugs, prolonged bed rest, or autonomic dysfunction, pressure falls, cerebral perfusion drops transiently, and the patient becomes lightheaded or syncopal, typically within the first steps away from the bed. CDC STEADI includes orthostatic blood pressure measurement in fall-risk assessment, with responses that include medication adjustment, hydration, and teaching slow staged position changes.
rationales.eli10: Standing up is a small circulatory emergency that your body normally solves before you notice it. The instant you rise, roughly half a liter of blood drifts downward into your legs, and the pressure available to your brain dips. Healthy vessels clamp down and the heart speeds up within a couple of heartbeats, so nothing happens. If illness, bed rest, or blood pressure medication weakens that response, the dip lasts several seconds instead, and those seconds happen while the person is standing at the bedside with nothing to hold. Taking the pressure lying and then standing is how you find the dip in advance, before it is discovered on the floor.

questions.stem: Which statement about side rails and fall prevention is accurate?

options.text: Raising all four full-length rails is the most dependable way to keep a confused patient in bed
Partial rails can support repositioning, whereas full rails used to confine a patient function as a restraint
Raised rails belong to universal fall precautions and should be fully up for every patient overnight
Rails count as restraints only when the patient states an objection to having them raised

rationales.whyCorrect: Under the federal restraint definition applied by CMS, a restraint is any device that restricts freedom of movement, so side rails raised specifically to prevent a patient from voluntarily leaving the bed meet that definition; classification turns on the purpose and effect of use, not on whether the patient objects or consents. A single rail or half rail used as a handhold supports independent turning and transfer and is not a restraint. Full rails also carry documented harms: patients who are determined to get up climb over them, converting a low fall into a fall from greater height, and the gaps among rail, mattress, and frame create recognized entrapment hazards. Safer approaches include a low bed, floor mats, and proactive rounding.
rationales.eli10: The same piece of metal can be a handle or a fence, and which one it is depends entirely on why it was raised. One rail up gives a patient something to pull against while rolling over, which supports movement. All four up to stop someone from leaving is a barrier, and confused patients who want out do not reason with barriers, they climb. Now the drop starts from the top of the rail rather than the edge of a low mattress, and there are gaps between rail, mattress, and frame where a limb or neck can wedge. That is why the regulation looks at intent: a device meant to keep someone in is a restraint whether or not they complained about it.

questions.stem: An older adult who fell last month has begun avoiding walking because of fear of falling. If this pattern continues over several months, which change would most likely result?

options.text: Fall risk decreases, because less time on the feet means fewer opportunities to fall
Fall risk increases, because reduced activity produces muscle weakness, deconditioning, and poorer balance
Fall risk dips and then returns to baseline, since strength recovers automatically once walking resumes
Fall risk is unchanged, because fear is psychological and does not alter physical capacity

rationales.whyCorrect: Fear of falling drives activity restriction, and disuse produces measurable loss of lower-extremity strength, endurance, and postural control within weeks, so the unavoidable transfers to the bathroom or kitchen are attempted on progressively weaker legs. questions.stem: An older adult takes 15 seconds to complete the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test. What does this result indicate?

options.text: Mobility is impaired at a level linked to increased fall risk, warranting further assessment
Performance falls within expected limits, so no additional fall-related follow-up is indicated
The result identifies an underlying neurologic disorder as the cause of the slow time
The person should remain on bed rest until lower-extremity strength has improved

rationales.whyCorrect: CDC STEADI sets the TUG threshold at 12 seconds or more as an indication of impaired mobility and increased fall risk, so 15 seconds is an abnormal screening result. A screening test estimates risk and directs further evaluation; it does not establish a diagnosis, so the appropriate next steps are completing the risk-factor assessment, including medication review, orthostatic blood pressure, gait and strength evaluation, and referring for targeted intervention such as physical therapy. Bed rest is the opposite of what the finding calls for, since it accelerates the deconditioning that the slow time reflects.
rationales.eli10: The TUG is a compressed obstacle course: rise from a chair, walk about ten feet, turn, walk back, sit. It packs strength, balance, turning, and reaction into one number, and CDC's cutoff is twelve seconds. Fifteen means the screen is positive, and that is all it means. A positive screen is a pointer, not an explanation, because the same slow time could come from arthritic knees, a sedating medication, poor vision, or fear of falling, and each of those needs a different fix. So the correct response is to keep looking, then treat what you find, usually with exercise and strengthening rather than with rest.

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates an injury-prevention strategy rather than a fall-prevention strategy?

options.text: Keeping the call light and frequently used personal items within the patient's reach
Reviewing the medication list for drugs known to increase fall risk
Placing a cushioned floor mat beside a bed kept in the lowest position
Orienting the patient to the room layout and bathroom location on admission

rationales.whyCorrect: Fall-prevention measures reduce the probability that a fall occurs, while injury-prevention measures reduce the severity of harm when one does occur; low beds, floor mats, hip protectors, and treatment of osteoporosis and vitamin D deficiency belong to the second group because they act only after a descent begins. Comprehensive programs need both, since falls cannot be eliminated in patients who are ill, medicated, and mobilizing, and because falls with injury, rather than falls overall, account for most resulting disability, prolonged stay, and death. Reporting fall rates alongside fall-with-injury rates reflects the same distinction.
rationales.eli10: Two separate jobs hide inside the phrase fall safety: stop the crash, and soften the crash. Clearing the path, reviewing sedating medications, and keeping the call light in reach all try to stop it. A padded mat next to a bed lowered to its floor position does nothing at all unless a fall is already happening, which is exactly what makes it injury prevention rather than fall prevention. It is the helmet, not the riding lesson. You want both, because in a hospital full of weak, medicated, unfamiliar-with-the-room patients, some falls will get through, and whether one of them breaks a hip depends on how far the body drops and what it lands on.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Fall-prevention measures reduce the probability that a fall occurs, while injury-prevention measures reduce the severity of harm when one does occur; low beds, floor mats, hip protectors, and treatment of osteoporosis and vitamin D deficiency belong to the second group because they act only after a descent begins. questions.stem: What is the primary reason that scheduled rounding addressing pain, toileting, and positioning lowers fall rates?

options.text: It ensures the fall-risk score is recalculated during each visit to the patient's room
It substitutes efficiently for individualized fall-risk assessment on short-staffed units
It shortens the interval between a fall and its discovery by nursing staff
It meets anticipated needs, especially toileting, before the patient tries to get up alone

rationales.whyCorrect: A large share of inpatient falls occurs during unassisted attempts to reach the bathroom, frequently at night, when urgency overrides a patient's stated willingness to wait for help. Structured rounding is proactive rather than reactive: by offering toileting, analgesia, repositioning, and placement of needed items on a predictable schedule, it removes the reason the patient would rise alone, rather than relying on the patient to call and wait. Shortening discovery time, as in option C, is a real secondary benefit but does not prevent the fall itself. AHRQ's toolkit therefore pairs rounding with universal fall precautions instead of depending on the call light.
rationales.eli10: A full bladder is not a negotiable request. Tell a patient a hundred times to call for help and they will still get up alone, at 3 a.m., in socks, towing an IV pole, because waiting is not something the body offers as an option. So the strategy is not to make people wait better, it is to arrive before the urgency builds. Checking in on a fixed rhythm and asking about the bathroom, pain, and position means the need is handled while it is still small. Rounding does also mean someone finds a fallen patient sooner, which is worth something, but that is damage control; the falls avoided are the ones that never started.

questions.stem: A unit documents a fall-risk score for every patient on every shift, yet its fall rate has not changed over the past year. Which explanation is most likely?

options.text: Scoring identifies risk but changes nothing by itself unless matched interventions are actually carried out
Standardized fall-risk scales lack validity and should be removed from fall-prevention programs entirely
A unit's fall rate reflects patient acuity and cannot be changed by unit-level practice improvements
Scores reduce falls only after a unit adopts a different scale, since tool choice drives program outcomes

rationales.whyCorrect: A fall-risk scale stratifies probability; it is an assessment step, not an intervention, and scoring without a linked, executed care plan is a well-documented reason fall programs stall. AHRQ's clinical pathway requires that each identified risk factor, such as impaired gait, urgent toileting needs, fall-risk-increasing medications, or altered mental status, generate a specific tailored response that is performed, communicated at handoff, and reassessed. Option D is wrong for a related reason: comparative studies have not shown one validated scale to be meaningfully more accurate than another, so switching tools does not fix an execution gap. The distance between documentation and action, not the arithmetic of the score, determines whether the rate moves.
rationales.eli10: A forecast of a ninety percent chance of rain keeps nobody dry. Someone still has to pick up the umbrella. A fall-risk score is that forecast, and the common failure mode in real units is that the number gets charted, the box gets checked for the audit, and nothing downstream changes, because the score does not name what to do. High risk from urgent toileting needs and high risk from a sedating sleep medication produce the same number but require completely different actions, one a two-hour bathroom schedule and the other a call to the prescriber. Swapping to a fancier scale would not help either, since no tool has proven clearly better than the rest at predicting who falls.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: A fall-risk scale stratifies probability; it is an assessment step, not an intervention, and scoring without a linked, executed care plan is a well-documented reason fall programs stall.
