questions.stem: Which statement reflects current evidence-based guidance on restraints and bed alarms in fall-prevention programs?

options.text: Physical restraints are the most effective option available for confused patients at high fall risk
Restraints are discouraged because immobility causes harm, and alarms alone have not reliably reduced falls
Restraints prevent injury by maintaining immobility, though skin breakdown may develop over time
Bed alarms should replace scheduled rounding, since alarms signal staff before a patient stands up

rationales.whyCorrect: AHRQ's hospital fall-prevention toolkit is explicit that routine restraint use represents poor care: immobility causes deconditioning, pressure injuries, incontinence, and agitation, and patients who struggle against restraints can sustain injuries more severe than the fall the restraint was meant to prevent. Restraint use is also legally constrained, requiring an order, a documented clinical justification, and time limits, and it is never a standing fall-prevention measure. Trials of bed alarms used as a stand-alone intervention, including a large randomized hospital trial, have not shown meaningful reductions in falls, because an alarm is a detection device that sounds after the patient is already rising and works only if a responder is close enough to intervene in time. Effective programs combine universal precautions, proactive rounding, mobility and strength interventions, and injury-reduction measures.
rationales.eli10: Both of these feel like solutions and neither carries its weight. Restraints trade one hazard for several: muscle wastes fast in someone who cannot move, skin breaks down, confusion worsens, and a patient fighting the straps can injure themselves worse than any fall would have. Alarms fail for a different reason. Watch what an alarm actually does in time order: the patient sits up, swings their legs over, the sensor triggers, and now the beep and the fall are racing each other down a hallway. If no one is within a few seconds' reach, the alarm simply announces what already happened. What works is unglamorous: check in before the need becomes urgent, keep the legs strong, lower the bed, pad the floor.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines a high-alert medication?

options.text: A medication involved in reported errors more often than most other drugs on the formulary
A medication that bears a heightened risk of significant patient harm when it is used in error
A medication that must be counted and co-signed each shift because it is a controlled substance
A medication with only a narrow margin between the usual dose and the toxic dose

rationales.whyCorrect: The Institute for Safe Medication Practices defines high-alert medications as drugs that bear a heightened risk of causing significant patient harm when they are used in error. ISMP explicitly notes that errors with these drugs are not necessarily more frequent; the consequences are simply more devastating, which is why option A states the most common misconception. Narrow therapeutic index (option D) and controlled-substance status (option C) overlap with the list but define neither its boundary nor its purpose. Insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, neuromuscular blocking agents, and concentrated electrolytes appear on ISMP's acute care list, and the recommended safeguards follow from severity: standardizing ordering and storage, restricting access, and using selective redundancies such as independent double checks.
rationales.eli10: Compare spilling water on the kitchen floor with spilling water on a laptop. You probably spill about as often in either place, but only one spill destroys something. High-alert medications are the laptop. What earns a drug that label is not how often people slip up with it, but how bad the outcome is when they do. Once you see that the defining feature is consequence rather than frequency, the extra guardrails make sense: locked storage, pre-mixed concentrations, and a second person checking are all ways of buying down a very expensive outcome.

ISMP explicitly notes that errors with these drugs are not necessarily more frequent; the consequences are simply more devastating, which is why option A states the most common misconception. questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of tall man lettering, as in predniSONE and prednisoLONE?

options.text: To signal that the generic name is being used rather than a proprietary brand name
To flag a medication as high-alert and therefore requiring an independent double check
To draw the reader's eye to the letters that differ between look-alike drug names
To show which syllable of the drug name should be stressed when it is spoken aloud

rationales.whyCorrect: Tall man lettering is a mixed-case labeling convention promoted by ISMP and the FDA in which the letters that distinguish two similar drug names are capitalized, forcing attention to the point of difference rather than the shared stem. It is applied to look-alike/sound-alike (LASA) name pairs on manufacturer labels, pharmacy shelf tags, order-entry screens, and automated dispensing cabinet displays. It is purely a name-differentiation strategy: it confers no high-alert designation, carries no information about generic versus brand naming, and says nothing about pronunciation.
rationales.eli10: When two words open the same way, your eye reads the beginning and lets the rest blur. You see "predni-" and your brain declares the job finished. Tall man lettering interrupts that shortcut by capitalizing only the part that differs, the way a highlighter marks the single line on a page you must not skim. The endings, not the beginnings, are what actually separate these drugs, so the formatting drags your attention to where the real information lives.

questions.stem: Which term describes building the most accurate possible list of every medication a patient is taking and formally comparing it with newly written orders at admission, transfer, and discharge?

options.text: Therapeutic drug monitoring
Formulary review
Medication reconciliation
Medication administration record audit

rationales.whyCorrect: Medication reconciliation is the structured process of compiling a best possible medication history and comparing it against current orders at each transition of care, then resolving discrepancies such as omissions, duplications, wrong doses, and drugs that should have been stopped. AHRQ identifies care transitions as the point where unintentional discrepancies most often arise, and reconciliation is the designed countermeasure. Therapeutic drug monitoring measures serum drug concentrations to guide dosing, formulary review governs which products an organization stocks, and an MAR audit examines documentation of doses already administered.
rationales.eli10: Picture moving house twice in one week. Boxes get loaded, unloaded, and reloaded, and unless someone stands at the door comparing the inventory list to what actually came off the truck, items vanish quietly and duplicates pile up. Medication reconciliation is that person at the door: "You arrived on five medicines, these new orders list four and one at a different strength. Which is intended?" Every hand-off, admission, transfer, discharge, is a doorway, and doorways are exactly where things go missing.

questions.stem: An order is handwritten as "insulin glargine 10U subcutaneous at bedtime." What is the most likely consequence if the abbreviation is misread?

options.text: It is read as 10 international units, a measure different from 10 units of insulin
It is read as 1 unit, because the "U" is mistaken for a decimal point after the 1
It is read as 100 units, because a handwritten "U" is easily mistaken for a zero
The route is read as intravenous, because "U" is commonly mistaken for "IV"

rationales.whyCorrect: "U" for unit appears on The Joint Commission's official "Do Not Use" list precisely because it is mistaken for a zero, for the number 4, or for "cc," and the required remedy is to write out the word "unit." Reading 10U as 100 units delivers a tenfold insulin overdose with real potential for severe hypoglycemia. Option B fails on its own logic: a stray loop can add a digit to a written dose but cannot delete one. Option D describes the hazard of a different prohibited abbreviation, "IU" for international unit, which is confused with IV or with the number 10. Option A poses no meaningful change, since insulin potency is standardized and "unit" and "international unit" denote the same measure for insulin.
rationales.eli10: Write a capital U and a zero side by side, quickly, the way anyone writes at 0300. Both are rounded loops, and when the U is jammed against the end of "10" it simply reads as one more digit. Nothing dramatic happens on the page; 10 quietly becomes 100. With insulin that is not a small overshoot, it is a dose that can drop blood sugar dangerously. The fix is deliberately low-tech: write the word "unit," because a word cannot be misread as a numeral.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: "U" for unit appears on The Joint Commission's official "Do Not Use" list precisely because it is mistaken for a zero, for the number 4, or for "cc," and the required remedy is to write out the word "unit." questions.stem: Which statement about the use of leading and trailing zeros in medication orders is accurate?

options.text: The leading zero should be omitted and a trailing zero added, so 0.5 mg is written .5 mg and 5 mg as 5.0 mg
Both zeros should be written, because the additional digits make the size of the dose easier to read
Trailing zeros are prohibited everywhere in the health record, while a leading zero is optional in orders
A leading zero always precedes a decimal point (0.5 mg), and a trailing zero never follows a whole number (5 mg)

rationales.whyCorrect: Both a missing leading zero and a trailing zero appear on The Joint Commission's official "Do Not Use" list because the decimal point is the most fragile mark in a written, faxed, or poorly displayed order. A leading zero anchors the eye so that a lost point still reads as a fraction, while a trailing zero creates the opposite exposure, since losing the point turns 5.0 into 50. Option C is wrong on both halves: the leading zero is required, not optional, and The Joint Commission permits a trailing zero in the narrow situations where precision must be demonstrated, such as laboratory results, lesion sizes on imaging reports, and catheter or tube sizes, but never in medication orders or medication-related documentation.
rationales.eli10: A decimal point is a speck of ink, and specks disappear in faxes, photocopies, and hurried handwriting. So test each number by asking what survives if the speck vanishes. Lose the point in ".5 mg" and you are left with 5 mg, ten times too much. Lose it in "5.0 mg" and you are left with 50 mg, again ten times too much. The zero in front rescues the number; the zero on the end inflates it. That asymmetry is the whole rule: one zero is a seatbelt, the other is a trap door.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Both a missing leading zero and a trailing zero appear on The Joint Commission's official "Do Not Use" list because the decimal point is the most fragile mark in a written, faxed, or poorly displayed order. A leading zero anchors the eye so that a lost point still reads as a fraction, while a trailing zero creates the opposite exposure, since losing the point turns 5.0 into 50. Option C is wrong on both halves: the leading zero is required, not optional, and The Joint Commission permits a trailing zero in the narrow situations where precision must be demonstrated, such as laboratory results, lesion sizes on imaging reports, and catheter or tube sizes, but never in medication orders or medication-related documentation.

questions.stem: What feature makes a double check of a high-alert medication a truly independent double check?

options.text: The second verifier is a pharmacist rather than another nurse, so the verification crosses professional disciplines
The second clinician watches the first clinician work through the calculation and confirms that each step is correct
The two clinicians complete the verification together at the bedside so that any discrepancy surfaces immediately
The second clinician verifies the drug, dose, and pump settings alone, without being told the first clinician's answer

rationales.whyCorrect: The detection power of a double check comes from cognitive independence: the second verifier works from the original order and the product in hand and reaches a conclusion before learning what the first clinician concluded. Options B and C describe observed or simultaneous checks, in which confirmation bias makes agreement close to automatic and the second review adds little. Option A describes a staffing arrangement, not the defining feature; a nurse-to-nurse check is fully valid when performed independently. ISMP advises reserving independent double checks for a small set of high-risk situations, because applying them broadly makes them perfunctory and erodes the very detection they are meant to provide.
rationales.eli10: If someone tells you the answer is 42 before you work the problem, your mind stops solving and starts looking for reasons to agree. That is not a check, it is an echo. A real second check means the other clinician goes to the original order and the actual vial or bag, works it out cold, and only then compares. Two people who genuinely solved it separately can disagree, and disagreement is the entire point. Two people where one merely nodded along produced one answer wearing two signatures.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: The detection power of a double check comes from cognitive independence: the second verifier works from the original order and the product in hand and reaches a conclusion before learning what the first clinician concluded. questions.stem: A unit uses barcode medication administration, but when a wristband will not scan, staff routinely scan a spare copy of the patient's barcode kept at the computer cart. Which effect is this workaround most likely to have?

options.text: It preserves the safety benefit, because the medication barcode is still scanned against the electronic order
It defeats the patient-identification check the system exists to perform, so wrong-patient errors reach the bedside
It is acceptable practice as long as the duplicate barcode was printed directly from that patient's own record
It has little measurable effect, because barcode scanning mainly documents the time at which a dose was given

rationales.whyCorrect: Barcode medication administration works by electronically matching the product in hand to the patient physically present at the moment of administration, and a detached duplicate label removes exactly that link. Where the duplicate came from is irrelevant, which is why option C is wrong: a label lying on a cart verifies only that a label exists, not that this patient is in this bed. AHRQ reports that BCMA can substantially reduce administration errors and potential adverse drug events, but that workarounds are common and are associated with markedly higher error risk. Scanning the drug alone still catches a wrong-product selection, so option D understates what the system does, and option A mistakes half the handshake for the whole of it.
rationales.eli10: A barcode scan is a handshake between two things: this medication and this person. Tape a spare label to the cart and the scanner shakes hands with a piece of paper, and paper agrees with absolutely everything. The screen flashes green, the documentation looks flawless, and the dose can still walk into the wrong room. Nothing about the technology failed here; the loop it was quietly closing was cut open by the workaround, and the reassuring green light is no longer telling you the person in front of you is the right one.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Barcode medication administration works by electronically matching the product in hand to the patient physically present at the moment of administration, and a detached duplicate label removes exactly that link. Where the duplicate came from is irrelevant, which is why option C is wrong: a label lying on a cart verifies only that a label exists, not that this patient is in this bed. questions.stem: Which example best illustrates a look-alike/sound-alike medication error?

options.text: A scheduled dose is given ninety minutes late because it had not yet arrived from the pharmacy
A patient prescribed hydrOXYzine receives hydrALAZINE pulled from the adjacent cabinet pocket
An oral liquid is drawn into a parenteral syringe and inadvertently administered intravenously
A full tablet is given after the prescriber reduced the order to one-half tablet that morning

rationales.whyCorrect: HydrOXYzine, an antihistamine, and hydrALAZINE, an antihypertensive, are a classic pair on the ISMP list of confused drug names and are displayed with tall man lettering for exactly that reason. Option B is a wrong-drug error produced by name similarity compounded by adjacent storage, the defining signature of a LASA event. The other options describe real but different error types: a delayed dose, a wrong-route error, and a wrong-dose error following an order change. Classifying the error correctly matters because the countermeasures differ, name differentiation and storage separation for LASA versus route-specific connectors for wrong-route events.
rationales.eli10: Say hydroxyzine and hydralazine quickly and they collapse into the same sound; look at them on a shelf and they occupy the same visual space. One relieves itching and anxiety, the other lowers blood pressure, so the swap is not a minor variation on the intended therapy. That is what look-alike/sound-alike means: the mistake originates in the name itself rather than in the dose, the route, or the timing. Ask where the confusion started, and the classification answers itself.

questions.stem: A nurse is about to administer a scheduled oral medication in a two-bed room. Which action best satisfies the right patient element of safe medication administration?

options.text: Matching two person-specific identifiers, such as full name and date of birth, to the record
Asking "You are Mr. Alvarez, correct?" and proceeding once the patient nods in agreement
Confirming the room number and bed letter against the medication administration record
Confirming with the family member at the bedside that this is the patient the drug is for

rationales.whyCorrect: Correct identification requires at least two identifiers that belong to the person rather than to a location, and room or bed number is explicitly unacceptable because patients are moved and beds are reassigned. Best practice is to have the patient state the identifiers, then match them against the medication administration record and the product label. Option B is a closed, leading question that a confused, sedated, or hard-of-hearing patient may affirm regardless of accuracy, and option D substitutes a proxy's recollection for verification against the record. Two independent person-specific matches are what make misidentification unlikely rather than merely improbable.
rationales.eli10: A room number describes furniture, and furniture does not get discharged, transferred, or swapped at 0200, but patients do. Asking "You are Mr. Alvarez, right?" is worse still, because you have handed over the answer and invited a polite nod. So use an open question and match two facts that travel with the person, name and date of birth, against the record. Requiring two matches works the way a key plus a password works: either one alone is guessable, both together rarely line up by accident.

questions.stem: A prescriber telephones an order for a high-alert medication to a nurse. Which nursing action best reduces the risk of a medication error?

options.text: Writing the order down, then reading it back to the prescriber, spelling the drug name and stating the dose
Repeating the order aloud from memory to the prescriber, then documenting it after the call has ended
Entering the order in the record and asking a second nurse to confirm that it was typed as intended
Accepting the order and asking the prescriber to countersign the entry within twenty-four hours

rationales.whyCorrect: The established sequence for verbal and telephone orders is write down or enter, read back, and obtain confirmation from the prescriber. Read-back is a long-standing Joint Commission expectation, introduced as National Patient Safety Goal 2 and now carried within the accreditation standards, and it is also an ISMP recommendation. The federal CMS hospital conditions of participation impose separate and narrower requirements: verbal orders are to be used infrequently and accepted only by persons authorized to do so by hospital policy (42 CFR 482.23(c)(3)), and all orders, including verbal orders, must be dated, timed, and authenticated promptly (42 CFR 482.24(c)(2)). Neither CMS section contains a read-back rule, so the practice is an accreditation and best-practice standard rather than a federal regulation. Reading back from memory (option B) simply replays whatever was misheard and leaves the record unwritten during the one moment the prescriber is still available. questions.stem: Which comparison of a medication error and an adverse drug event is accurate?

options.text: They name a single occurrence from two viewpoints: the prescriber records an error and the patient experiences an adverse drug event
A medication error is an adverse drug event that staff intercepted before it reached the patient, so every error is a subset of ADEs
An adverse drug event is any breakdown in the medication-use process, whether or not the drug reached the patient and caused harm
A medication error is a process failure that need not cause harm, while an adverse drug event is harm that need not involve error

rationales.whyCorrect: The two terms are defined on different axes. A medication error is a failure anywhere in the medication-use process, prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, administering, or monitoring, and it is classified by the process breakdown rather than the outcome, which is why most errors are intercepted or cause no injury. An adverse drug event is defined by harm to a patient involving a medication, and only a portion of ADEs are error-related; a first-ever allergic reaction to a correctly prescribed and correctly administered drug is an ADE with no error at all. Neither category contains the other, so options A, B, and C each collapse one axis onto the other. The overlapping region, preventable ADEs, is the subset that AHRQ and medication safety systems specifically target.
rationales.eli10: Draw two circles that partly overlap. One circle is "something went wrong in the process," the other is "a medicine hurt the patient." Many process failures are caught at the pharmacy or the bedside and never touch anyone, so they sit in the first circle alone. And a person can react badly to a drug that was chosen and given perfectly, which lands in the second circle with no mistake anywhere. Only the overlap is both harmful and preventable, and that slice is where safety work concentrates because it is the part anyone can actually shrink.

questions.stem: After several serious events involving concentrated potassium chloride vials stored on nursing units, a hospital considers four responses. Which change is most likely to produce the largest and most durable reduction in harm?

options.text: Removing concentrated potassium chloride from floor stock so only diluted solutions reach the units
Affixing a bright auxiliary warning label to every vial of concentrated potassium chloride
Requiring every nurse to complete annual competency education on potassium chloride administration
Posting a laminated potassium dilution reference chart at every medication preparation station

rationales.whyCorrect: Interventions differ systematically in reliability. Warning labels, posted references, and annual education all depend on a busy clinician noticing and recalling information at the exact moment of action, which places them at the weak end of the hierarchy of intervention effectiveness. Removing the concentrated product is a constraint operating at the forcing-function level: the error becomes physically impossible on the unit rather than merely discouraged, and it stays impossible regardless of staffing, fatigue, or turnover. Restricting access to high-alert medications and supplying standardized, ready-to-administer concentrations are core ISMP recommendations, and withdrawal of concentrated potassium chloride from floor stock is the canonical example, adopted broadly after fatal undiluted-injection events. Labeling and education remain useful supporting layers but are the weakest defenses when relied on alone.
rationales.eli10: You can post a warning sign at the top of a staircase, or you can install a gate. The sign works only when a tired, distracted person happens to look up; the gate works even when nobody looks at all. Taking concentrated potassium off the unit is the gate, because no one can grab the dangerous vial by mistake when the dangerous vial is not in the building. Training and labels still matter, but they draw on attention and memory, and attention and memory are precisely what a hard shift spends first.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a near miss (also called a close call) in health care?

options.text: An error that reached the patient and caused an injury requiring additional treatment
A decline in the patient's condition produced by the natural progression of the underlying illness
An error that could have injured the patient but did not, because of interception or chance
A deviation from unit policy discovered by a manager during a scheduled quality audit

rationales.whyCorrect: AHRQ describes a near miss as an unsafe situation that is indistinguishable from a preventable adverse event in every respect except outcome: the patient was exposed to a hazardous situation but was not harmed, either through luck or through early detection. Two features define it, that a genuine error or unsafe situation occurred, and that the absence of injury was not guaranteed by the design of the system. Worsening from the disease process itself is not a safety event at all, and a policy deviation found on audit describes how something was discovered rather than whether harm was averted.
rationales.eli10: Picture knocking a glass off the counter and catching it an inch above the floor. Nothing broke, but the knock still happened, and next time your hand may be slower. That caught glass is the near miss: the mistake was real, and only a quick catch or plain luck stood between it and damage. The event that already landed and shattered is a different category, and so is a glass that simply wore out on its own.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: AHRQ describes a near miss as an unsafe situation that is indistinguishable from a preventable adverse event in every respect except outcome: the patient was exposed to a hazardous situation but was not harmed, either through luck or through early detection. questions.stem: What distinguishes an adverse event from other undesirable patient outcomes?

options.text: The injury always follows a clinician's failure to comply with a written protocol
The event reaches the patient but causes no measurable injury or added treatment
The injury is caused by medical care or its management rather than by the underlying disease
The injury is confirmed only after a formal root cause analysis has been completed

rationales.whyCorrect: AHRQ defines an adverse event as harm resulting from medical care rather than from the patient's underlying condition. Causation by care, not culpability, is the criterion, which is why AHRQ further sorts adverse events into preventable ones (caused by error or by failure to apply a known prevention strategy), ameliorable ones (not preventable, but the harm could have been reduced), and those involving negligence. Anaphylaxis on first exposure to a correctly prescribed and correctly administered drug is an adverse event with no error and no protocol breach, which shows why rule-breaking cannot be part of the definition.
rationales.eli10: Someone breaks a leg skiing, so that injury came from skiing. If the cast is then applied too tightly and the foot is damaged, the second injury came from the treatment. Adverse event means tracing the harm back to the care rather than to the illness that brought the person in. Nothing in that trace requires anyone to have broken a rule, and an event with no injury at all does not qualify no matter how alarming it felt.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: AHRQ defines an adverse event as harm resulting from medical care rather than from the patient's underlying condition. questions.stem: Which term describes a patient safety event that reaches the patient and results in death, severe harm, or permanent harm?

options.text: Sentinel event
Close call (near miss)
No-harm event
Hazardous condition

rationales.whyCorrect: The Joint Commission's current Sentinel Event Policy defines a sentinel event as a patient safety event, not primarily related to the natural course of the patient's illness or underlying condition, that reaches a patient and results in death, severe harm regardless of the duration of that harm, or permanent harm regardless of its severity. The term signals an event serious enough to demand immediate investigation and response, and The Joint Commission additionally designates certain occurrences, such as wrong-site surgery or infant abduction, as sentinel regardless of the outcome. The other three terms occupy lower rungs of the same ladder: a no-harm event reaches the patient without injuring them, a close call does not reach the patient, and a hazardous condition is a circumstance that raises the probability of an event before any event has occurred.

The other three terms name quieter alarms further down the same ladder, sorted by how close the danger came: never reached the person, reached them without hurting them, or was simply a trap sitting there waiting.

questions.stem: Which example illustrates an error of omission rather than an error of commission?

options.text: A dressing is changed on the wrong extremity because the site was not confirmed first
A specimen is labeled with another patient's name because the identifiers were not verified
An enteral feeding is connected to the wrong line because the tubing was not traced first
An ordered postoperative neurovascular check is never performed because it was missed at handoff

rationales.whyCorrect: AHRQ defines an error as any act of commission, meaning doing something wrong, or omission, meaning failing to do the right thing, that exposes a patient to a potentially hazardous situation. An assessment that is ordered and never performed is a failure to act, so it is an omission, whereas mislabeling a specimen, misconnecting tubing, and treating the wrong site are all actions that were carried out incorrectly. The distinction has practical consequences: an omission usually shows up only as a blank where an entry should have been, rather than as a positive entry, so it is easier to overlook and tends to be reported less often than a commission.
rationales.eli10: Think about leaving the house. Forgetting to lock the door is an omission, because the right action never happened. Locking the neighbor's door by mistake is a commission, because an action did happen, just the wrong one. Every option here has a cause involving something not being checked, so the trick is to ignore the cause and ask only one thing: did a required action go undone, or did a wrong action get carried out?

questions.stem: What is the primary reason patient safety programs actively encourage staff to report near misses?

options.text: Near misses reveal the same system weaknesses as harmful events while no patient has been injured
Near misses occur less often than harmful events, so each report is a rare and notable signal
Near-miss reports identify which individual staff member should be held accountable for the lapse
Near-miss counts are the most accurate available measure of an organization's true rate of harm

rationales.whyCorrect: Near misses arise from the same latent system vulnerabilities as events that injure patients, but they are far more numerous and carry no injury, so they yield information about thin defenses at essentially no cost to the patient. AHRQ states that reporting systems are best used as a way of identifying issues that require further, more detailed investigation, which rules out treating report counts as a harm rate or as a disciplinary instrument. Analyzing why an error was intercepted is equally valuable, because it shows which existing barriers are actually functioning and should be reinforced.
rationales.eli10: Smoke detectors are useful precisely because smoke arrives before flames. A near miss is the smoke: the fire has not started, but the faulty wiring is already in the wall. An organization that only investigates after someone is burned throws away every free warning it was given, and there are always far more smoke moments than fires, which is what makes them such a rich source of information.

questions.stem: Which comparison of errors and adverse events is accurate?

options.text: Every error produces an adverse event, although only the preventable ones require formal reporting
Adverse events are by definition preventable, whereas errors are frequently unavoidable in complex care
Some errors cause no harm and some adverse events involve no error, so the categories only partly overlap
An occurrence counts as an error only once harm to the patient has been objectively confirmed

rationales.whyCorrect: The two terms are defined by different criteria: an error is a flawed act or omission that exposes a patient to a hazard, while an adverse event is an injury caused by medical care. Because the criteria differ, the sets only partially intersect; many errors are intercepted or inconsequential, producing near misses and no-harm events, while some adverse events, such as an unpredictable first-exposure drug reaction, follow entirely correct care. Recognizing the intersection is what lets an organization isolate preventable adverse events, the subset where an error caused actual injury, as its primary improvement target.
rationales.eli10: Draw two circles that partly cross. One holds mistakes; the other holds patients hurt by their care. Many mistakes get caught or turn out to be harmless, so they sit in the mistakes-only crescent. Some patients are hurt by a rare reaction nobody could have predicted, so that sits in the harm-only crescent. The slice where the circles overlap, mistakes that actually injured someone, is the piece safety teams work hardest to shrink.

questions.stem: Which comparison of root cause analysis (RCA) and failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) is accurate?

options.text: Both are retrospective reviews, but RCA is reserved for near misses and FMEA for sentinel events
RCA determines which individual was responsible, while FMEA determines which policy was violated
FMEA is conducted after harm reaches a patient, while RCA is conducted before a new process launches
RCA looks backward at an event that occurred; FMEA looks forward at how a process could fail

rationales.whyCorrect: RCA is retrospective, a structured team investigation of an event that already happened, tracing contributing factors from the immediate actions back to system causes and concluding in a corrective action plan. FMEA is prospective, in which a team maps a process that has not yet failed, predicts the ways each step could fail, estimates severity and likelihood, and mitigates the highest-risk failure modes before patients are exposed. Both methods are explicitly system-focused rather than person-focused, which is why any option framing them around identifying a culpable individual or a violated rule misstates their purpose.
rationales.eli10: RCA is watching game film after a loss and asking what actually went wrong and why the breakdown was possible. FMEA is walking the field before the game and asking where things could break so they can be fixed in advance. One faces the past, one faces the future. Neither method exists to decide whose fault something was, which is the fastest way to eliminate the blame-flavored options.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: RCA is retrospective, a structured team investigation of an event that already happened, tracing contributing factors from the immediate actions back to system causes and concluding in a corrective action plan. FMEA is prospective, in which a team maps a process that has not yet failed, predicts the ways each step could fail, estimates severity and likelihood, and mitigates the highest-risk failure modes before patients are exposed. Both methods are explicitly system-focused rather than person-focused, which is why any option framing them around identifying a culpable individual or a violated rule misstates their purpose.

questions.stem: A patient receives a scheduled medication that had been discontinued earlier that day and shows no ill effects. What is the primary purpose of completing the facility's incident (occurrence) report?

options.text: To satisfy a federal requirement that every medication event be reported directly to the FDA
To create a permanent entry in the patient's medical record describing the deviation from the order
To establish a written basis for deciding which employee should receive corrective discipline
To supply the organization with analyzable data about the system problems that allowed the event

rationales.whyCorrect: An incident or occurrence report is an internal risk management and quality improvement document whose purpose is to surface events so that patterns can be analyzed and system defenses corrected, not to assign discipline. It is not part of the legal medical record; the chart should contain the objective clinical facts, meaning the drug given, the assessment, the provider notification, and the patient's response, without any reference to a report having been filed. Direct reporting to the FDA through MedWatch applies to suspected product-related adverse events and product problems, not to every medication event that occurs.
rationales.eli10: Two separate notebooks are in play. The chart is the story of the patient: what was given, how they responded, who was notified. The incident report is the organization's own maintenance log: what broke in our process so we can repair it. Writing "incident report filed" into the chart blurs a care record into a repair record, and afterward neither notebook does its job cleanly.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: An incident or occurrence report is an internal risk management and quality improvement document whose purpose is to surface events so that patterns can be analyzed and system defenses corrected, not to assign discipline. questions.stem: A pharmacy technician notices that a look-alike vial of the wrong drug has been placed in a prepared order and removes it before the dose leaves the pharmacy. Which classification best fits this occurrence?

options.text: No-harm event, because the patient was not injured by the dose that was prepared
Near miss, because an error occurred but was intercepted before it reached the patient
Hazardous condition, because look-alike vials are stored next to each other in the pharmacy
Preventable adverse event, because an established safeguard failed during dose preparation

rationales.whyCorrect: A real error occurred when the wrong vial was pulled, but a system defense caught it and the medication never left the pharmacy, which is exactly the definition of a near miss or close call. A no-harm event requires that the event reach the patient without producing injury, and an adverse event requires actual harm caused by care, so neither fits an intercepted dose. The look-alike storage arrangement is genuinely a hazardous condition, but that term names the standing circumstance that raises risk, not the specific occurrence being classified here.
rationales.eli10: Follow the vial. It was pulled incorrectly, which is the error; a person caught it, which is the interception; and it never left the pharmacy, which is why it is a near miss rather than something that reached the patient. The crowded shelf where two look-alike vials sit side by side is a separate finding, the trap that was waiting before anyone stepped in it, and traps and trips get classified under different names.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: A real error occurred when the wrong vial was pulled, but a system defense caught it and the medication never left the pharmacy, which is exactly the definition of a near miss or close call. questions.stem: A root cause analysis of repeated near misses finds that two different concentrations of the same drug are stocked side by side on a unit. Which action in the improvement plan would most likely prevent recurrence?

options.text: Send a unit-wide email reminding staff to read concentration labels carefully before administering
Remove the higher concentration from unit stock so only one concentration is available
Post a bright warning sign on the shelf where the two concentrations are stored together
Require every nurse to complete an annual education module on reading drug labels

rationales.whyCorrect: The RCA2 action hierarchy ranks corrective actions by how heavily they depend on human vigilance. Strong actions change the system itself by removing the hazard, forcing a safe path, or standardizing and simplifying the process; intermediate actions include alerts, checklists, and independent verification; weaker actions include warnings and labels, new policies, and training. Removing one concentration from unit stock eliminates the confusable choice entirely, the same reasoning that removed concentrated potassium chloride from floor stock decades ago, and RCA2 advises at least one strong or intermediate action per contributing cause because weaker actions alone rarely sustain improvement.
rationales.eli10: If two nearly identical bottles keep getting confused, one option is taping a sign to the shelf and hoping every tired person reads it every single time. The other is taking one bottle off the shelf so the mix-up becomes impossible. Signs, emails, and yearly modules all route through a human's attention at the worst possible moment. Changing the shelf itself never gets tired or distracted, which is why that class of fix ranks as strong.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: The RCA2 action hierarchy ranks corrective actions by how heavily they depend on human vigilance. Strong actions change the system itself by removing the hazard, forcing a safe path, or standardizing and simplifying the process; intermediate actions include alerts, checklists, and independent verification; weaker actions include warnings and labels, new policies, and training. questions.stem: Six months after a hospital introduces a confidential, nonpunitive reporting system, one unit's number of submitted event reports doubles while its independently measured harm rate is unchanged. Which interpretation of this pattern is most defensible?

options.text: Care quality on the unit has deteriorated, so the reporting system should be paused for review
Willingness to report has likely increased, so the rise reflects better detection, not more errors
The measured harm rate must be wrong, since report counts are the most reliable harm measure
The submitted reports are largely false, so stricter criteria are needed for what may be entered

rationales.whyCorrect: AHRQ notes that event reports are subject to selection bias because of their voluntary nature and capture only a fraction of the events found by chart review or direct observation, so counts measure reporting behavior at least as much as event frequency. Reports supply a numerator without a trustworthy denominator, which is why AHRQ specifically criticizes organizations that celebrate either a rise or a fall in report volume without first establishing what drove the change. A doubling of reports alongside a stable, independently measured harm rate is the expected signature of an improved reporting culture rather than evidence of deteriorating care.
rationales.eli10: If a town hands out rain gauges and suddenly records twice as much rain, the sky did not change; the counting did. Event reports behave the same way, because when people stop fearing punishment, events that were always happening finally get written down. That is precisely why harm has to be measured separately, through chart review or trigger tools, instead of being inferred from how many reports arrive.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: AHRQ notes that event reports are subject to selection bias because of their voluntary nature and capture only a fraction of the events found by chart review or direct observation, so counts measure reporting behavior at least as much as event frequency. Reports supply a numerator without a trustworthy denominator, which is why AHRQ specifically criticizes organizations that celebrate either a rise or a fall in report volume without first establishing what drove the change. A doubling of reports alongside a stable, independently measured harm rate is the expected signature of an improved reporting culture rather than evidence of deteriorating care.

questions.stem: Which statement accurately describes the obligations that follow a sentinel event in a Joint Commission-accredited hospital?

options.text: Self-reporting to The Joint Commission is voluntary, but the organization must still complete a comprehensive systematic analysis and action plan within 45 business days
Federal law requires that every sentinel event and every near miss be reported to The Joint Commission within 45 business days of its discovery
Confidentiality protections for patient safety work done with a Patient Safety Organization arise from hospital policy rather than from federal statute
Disclosure of the harm to the patient and family should be withheld until the analysis is complete and has been reviewed by legal counsel

rationales.whyCorrect: Under the current Sentinel Event Policy, an accredited organization is strongly encouraged but not required to report a sentinel event to The Joint Commission; what accreditation does require is a thorough and credible comprehensive systematic analysis and corrective action plan prepared within 45 business days of the event or of becoming aware of it. Confidentiality and privilege for patient safety work product shared with a Patient Safety Organization come from federal statute, the Patient Safety and Quality Improvement Act of 2005, not from an internal policy an organization writes for itself. Prompt disclosure of harm to the patient and family is a professional and ethical expectation reinforced by accreditation standards and, in many states, by law, so it is not held until an investigation concludes.
rationales.eli10: Three different rule-makers appear in this question, and separating them is the whole exercise. Congress writes statute, which is where the confidentiality protection for work shared with a Patient Safety Organization comes from. An accreditor writes standards a hospital agrees to follow to keep its seal of approval, which is where the analysis deadline comes from. Professional ethics says be honest with the patient promptly. Only one option pairs every rule with the rule-maker that actually issued it.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Under the current Sentinel Event Policy, an accredited organization is strongly encouraged but not required to report a sentinel event to The Joint Commission; what accreditation does require is a thorough and credible comprehensive systematic analysis and corrective action plan prepared within 45 business days of the event or of becoming aware of it. questions.stem: Which statement best defines an organization's patient safety culture?

options.text: The shared values, beliefs, and norms among staff that shape how they act and behave regarding safety.
The written policies, procedures, and accreditation standards a facility must follow to keep its license.
The measured rate of adverse events and infections a facility reports over a defined time period.
The formal chain of command staff use to escalate unsafe conditions to administrators and regulators.

rationales.whyCorrect: AHRQ defines patient safety culture as the values, beliefs, and norms shared by clinicians and staff that influence their actions and behaviors around safety. Culture is what people actually believe and do, which is distinct from the written rules (policy), the outcome numbers (adverse event rates), and the reporting structure (chain of command). The distinction is practical, not academic: an organization can hold flawless policies on paper and still have a weak safety culture, which is why culture is measured through staff perception surveys rather than through document review.
rationales.eli10: A highway has a posted speed limit, and that sign is the policy. The culture is how fast people on that road actually drive, and whether a passenger feels comfortable saying 'ease up.' Those two things can be very far apart. Safety culture is the unwritten 'how we really operate here,' and it is what governs behavior at 3 a.m. when no supervisor is watching.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: AHRQ defines patient safety culture as the values, beliefs, and norms shared by clinicians and staff that influence their actions and behaviors around safety. Culture is what people actually believe and do, which is distinct from the written rules (policy), the outcome numbers (adverse event rates), and the reporting structure (chain of command). The distinction is practical, not academic: an organization can hold flawless policies on paper and still have a weak safety culture, which is why culture is measured through staff perception surveys rather than through document review.

questions.stem: Which set of categories does the just culture framework use to classify staff behavior involved in an unsafe event?

options.text: Minor, moderate, and major, graded by how much harm actually reached the patient.
Active failure, latent condition, and organizational drift, graded by where in the system it began.
Preventable, unpreventable, and unavoidable, graded by how predictable the outcome was clinically.
Human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior, graded by the choice behind the action.

rationales.whyCorrect: Just culture sorts behavior into human error (an unintentional slip, lapse, or mistake), at-risk behavior (a shortcut taken where the risk is not recognized or is mistakenly believed to be justified), and reckless behavior (conscious disregard of a substantial and unjustifiable risk). The organizational response is matched to the behavior, not to the severity of what happened to the patient. Grading by harm is precisely what the framework rejects, because identical behavior can produce a near miss one day and a death the next depending on factors outside the clinician's control.
rationales.eli10: Three drivers each rear-end the same car. One hit a patch of black ice. One was following a little close because everyone on that road does and it never felt dangerous. One was racing a friend. The dented bumper looks identical in all three cases, but treating those drivers the same would be indefensible. Just culture asks what choice the person made, not how unlucky the outcome happened to be.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Just culture sorts behavior into human error (an unintentional slip, lapse, or mistake), at-risk behavior (a shortcut taken where the risk is not recognized or is mistakenly believed to be justified), and reckless behavior (conscious disregard of a substantial and unjustifiable risk). questions.stem: What is the primary focus of human factors engineering as it is applied in health care?

options.text: Designing tasks, equipment, and environments to fit human capabilities and limitations.
Measuring how much clinical content staff retain after completing annual education modules.
Identifying which individual acted closest to the patient so accountability can be assigned.
Setting staffing ratios that satisfy state licensure and accreditation survey requirements.

rationales.whyCorrect: Human factors engineering studies how people interact with tools, tasks, and their physical and organizational environment, then redesigns the work so the safe action is also the easiest and most natural one. It starts from the premise that human attention, memory, and vigilance are limited in predictable ways, so the system should absorb that limitation rather than demand perfection from the user. This is why human factors interventions target design and workflow rather than exhortation, willpower, or additional knowledge alone.
rationales.eli10: A USB-C cable plugs in no matter which way you are holding it, in the dark, one-handed. Someone made it symmetrical on purpose because they knew users would fumble it. That is human factors: instead of printing 'insert correctly' on the cable, the designer removed the wrong way. In hospitals the same reasoning gets applied to pump screens, tubing connectors, alarm sounds, and how a supply room is laid out.

questions.stem: Which comparison between a purely "blame-free" culture and a just culture is accurate?

options.text: Both hold staff answerable for every unsafe outcome, but a just culture adds mandatory remedial training.
A blame-free culture examines system design, whereas a just culture examines only individual decisions.
Both encourage open reporting, but a just culture still holds staff answerable for knowingly reckless choices.
A blame-free culture applies only to licensed clinicians, whereas a just culture applies to all employees.

rationales.whyCorrect: A blame-free environment removes the fear of punishment so that people will report events and hazards, which is essential but incomplete: taken alone it leaves no mechanism for addressing genuinely reckless conduct. Just culture preserves the protection for honest human error and system-induced at-risk behavior while retaining accountability for conscious disregard of substantial, known risk. Reporting safety and personal accountability are therefore complementary rather than opposed, which is why AHRQ and safety scholars describe just culture as the balance point between a purely punitive and a purely blame-free response.
rationales.eli10: A coach who never criticizes a missed shot is doing something smart, because players who fear the sideline stop taking shots at all. But 'we never say anything to anyone' collapses the moment someone deliberately trips an opponent. Just culture is the coach who says: missed shots, tell me what you saw, no consequences; deliberate tripping, that we address. Safe to speak, still answerable for choices.

questions.stem: In a high reliability organization, what does the principle of deference to expertise mean in day-to-day practice?

options.text: The most senior clinician present makes the final call, because seniority reflects accumulated experience.
Staff follow the written protocol instead of local judgment whenever a developing situation becomes ambiguous.
Decision making shifts toward whoever holds the most relevant knowledge of the situation, regardless of rank.
Outside consultants review each unit's safety data and set that unit's improvement priorities each year.

rationales.whyCorrect: AHRQ PSNet describes deference to expertise as the recognition that the person with the greatest knowledge of a developing situation may not be the person with the highest status or seniority, so authority migrates toward frontline knowledge as a problem unfolds. Option A describes a steep authority gradient, which high reliability organizations deliberately flatten; option B confuses the principle with rigid rule-following and ignores the companion principles of sensitivity to operations and commitment to resilience; option D misreads "expertise" as external consultants rather than situational knowledge. The principle only functions when staff at every level believe speaking up is safe and will be heard.
rationales.eli10: On a flight deck, rank does not overrule the fuel system. If the person who actually knows how that system behaves is not the captain, a well-run crew still listens to them, and the captain's job becomes making sure that voice reaches the decision. On a unit, the aide who has been at the bedside for eight hours may hold the single detail that changes the plan. Deference to expertise means the operative question is 'who actually knows?' rather than 'who outranks whom?'
rationales.distractorAnalysis: AHRQ PSNet describes deference to expertise as the recognition that the person with the greatest knowledge of a developing situation may not be the person with the highest status or seniority, so authority migrates toward frontline knowledge as a problem unfolds. questions.stem: Which question best reflects a systems (human factors) approach rather than a person approach to an unsafe situation?

options.text: Who was assigned to that area, and has that person been counseled about this before?
Which written policy did the staff member fail to follow even though training was completed?
What conditions in the work environment made this action seem like the reasonable choice at the time?
How can this individual be motivated to be more careful during high-volume shifts?

rationales.whyCorrect: The systems approach rests on local rationality: people generally act in ways that make sense given the information, time, tools, and pressures available to them in the moment. Asking what made the action seem reasonable surfaces latent design flaws, competing production demands, and confusing equipment that a person-focused inquiry never reaches. The other three questions terminate at the individual and characteristically generate counseling and retraining while leaving the hazardous conditions fully intact for the next clinician who walks into them.
rationales.eli10: If ten different people trip on the same step, you can keep telling each one to watch their feet, or you can go look at the step. The systems question is 'what is it about this step?' Human factors specialists ask that deliberately, because correcting the walker never fixes the stair, and the eleventh person is already on their way up.

questions.stem: High reliability organizations are often described as "preoccupied with failure." What does this principle actually mean?

options.text: They accept that failure is inevitable and concentrate resources on responding after harm occurs.
They treat small glitches and weak warning signals as clues pointing to larger system weaknesses.
They emphasize individual failure rates in evaluations so staff stay motivated to avoid mistakes.
They suspend high-risk procedures until published evidence shows the failure rate is acceptably low.

rationales.whyCorrect: Preoccupation with failure means the organization stays alert to minor irregularities and near misses instead of dismissing them as noise, because small signals often expose the same fault lines that later produce serious harm. AHRQ describes the stance as one in which the absence of accidents produces heightened vigilance rather than complacency, making it anticipatory rather than reactive and system-focused rather than a tally of individual failure rates. The principle depends entirely on culture, since weak signals only reach leadership if frontline staff believe it is safe and worthwhile to report them.
rationales.eli10: A pilot who hears one unfamiliar rattle does not wait for the engine to quit before investigating. That rattle is free information about something bending before it breaks. Preoccupation with failure means being the kind of team that chases the rattle, and equally the kind of team where the newest member feels entirely comfortable saying 'I heard something odd.' One without the other does not work.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Preoccupation with failure means the organization stays alert to minor irregularities and near misses instead of dismissing them as noise, because small signals often expose the same fault lines that later produce serious harm. AHRQ describes the stance as one in which the absence of accidents produces heightened vigilance rather than complacency, making it anticipatory rather than reactive and system-focused rather than a tally of individual failure rates. The principle depends entirely on culture, since weak signals only reach leadership if frontline staff believe it is safe and worthwhile to report them.

questions.stem: Which example is a true forcing function rather than a weaker, human-dependent safeguard?

options.text: A gas connector shaped so that only the matching oxygen line can physically attach to the port.
A rule requiring two staff members to independently verify a setting before it is used.
A bright red label placed on the shelf where a high-alert product is stored.
An annual competency module reviewing the hazards of connecting the wrong line.

rationales.whyCorrect: A forcing function is a design constraint that makes the unsafe action impossible to complete, so safety no longer depends on the user noticing, remembering, or choosing correctly. Incompatible connector geometry blocks the wrong connection regardless of how rushed, fatigued, or distracted the user is. Labels, independent double checks, and education are legitimate safeguards, but each still requires a human to attend and comply correctly every time; on the intervention effectiveness hierarchy the connector is a strong action while the other three range from intermediate to weak.
rationales.eli10: A diesel nozzle is too wide to fit the filler neck on a gasoline car. You can be exhausted, on the phone, and holding it with one hand, and it still will not go in. Nobody had to read anything or remember anything. Compare that to a sticker on the pump reading 'check your fuel type,' which works only if you look at it and only if you are not already thinking about something else.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: A forcing function is a design constraint that makes the unsafe action impossible to complete, so safety no longer depends on the user noticing, remembering, or choosing correctly. Incompatible connector geometry blocks the wrong connection regardless of how rushed, fatigued, or distracted the user is. questions.stem: A hospital's results from the AHRQ Surveys on Patient Safety Culture (SOPS) show a notably low score on the "communication openness" composite. What does this finding most directly indicate?

options.text: The hospital's adverse event rate exceeds the national benchmark for facilities of its size.
Staffing levels are too low for staff to complete required communication with families.
Handoff documentation is being completed incorrectly when patients transfer between units.
Staff do not feel free to speak up or to question the decisions of those with more authority.

rationales.whyCorrect: In the SOPS Hospital Survey 2.0, the communication openness composite is built from items asking whether staff speak up when they see something that may harm a patient, whether they speak up when someone with more authority is doing something unsafe, whether those with more authority are receptive when they do, and whether staff are afraid to ask questions. It is therefore a perception measure of psychological safety, not a measure of event rates, documentation accuracy, or staffing adequacy, each of which SOPS captures in separate composites such as staffing and work pace or handoffs and information exchange. Reading the composite correctly matters because the indicated remedy is leadership behavior and speak-up norms rather than a new form or a new report.
rationales.eli10: This survey is essentially asking every employee, anonymously, 'if you saw something wrong, would you actually say it out loud, even to someone above you?' A low score means a lot of people quietly answered no. That is not a report that harm has occurred yet; it means the batteries have been taken out of the smoke detector, and that is worth fixing before there is smoke.

questions.stem: A nurse routinely jots handoff information on a scrap of paper instead of using the unit's standardized handoff tool, a shortcut most of the staff use because the tool takes a long time to load. No harm has resulted. Under a just culture framework, which response fits this behavior?

options.text: Discipline the nurse formally, since a required safe process was knowingly bypassed.
Coach the nurse and address the system conditions that make the shortcut worthwhile.
Console the nurse, since this was an unintentional slip caused by time pressure.
Take no action toward the nurse, since no patient was harmed by the shortcut.

rationales.whyCorrect: This is at-risk behavior: a deliberate deviation whose risk has become invisible because the entire unit does it, the pattern known as normalization of deviance. Just culture answers at-risk behavior with coaching plus removal of the incentive for the shortcut, reserving discipline for reckless conduct and consoling for honest human error. Because the slow tool is what drives the drift, coaching alone will not hold; the behavior will simply recur with the next nurse facing the same load-time delay.
rationales.eli10: If every roommate cuts across the freshly mopped floor because the long way takes forever, singling out one of them changes nothing for a week at most. The durable answer has two parts: talk to the person, and then move the mop bucket or prop the other door so the safe route stops being the annoying route. That pairing, conversation plus system change, is exactly how just culture handles shortcuts.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: This is at-risk behavior: a deliberate deviation whose risk has become invisible because the entire unit does it, the pattern known as normalization of deviance. Just culture answers at-risk behavior with coaching plus removal of the incentive for the shortcut, reserving discipline for reckless conduct and consoling for honest human error. Because the slow tool is what drives the drift, coaching alone will not hold; the behavior will simply recur with the next nurse facing the same load-time delay.

questions.stem: On a busy unit, nearly every nurse carries a hand-written cheat sheet because the approved electronic reference requires six clicks and about 40 seconds to open. From a human factors perspective, what does this widespread workaround most likely signal?

options.text: A safe adaptation needing no follow-up, since staff reach the same information by a faster route.
A knowledge deficit among staff that is best corrected by assigning a refresher education module.
An accountability problem requiring individual follow-up, since the expected resource is clearly posted.
A mismatch between the designed process and the real demands of the work, indicating a need for redesign.

rationales.whyCorrect: When a workaround is nearly universal rather than isolated, it is evidence about the design and not about the people: work-as-imagined does not match work-as-done. Framing it as a knowledge or accountability problem misdiagnoses the cause and drives the practice underground, where it becomes invisible to the people who could fix it. Leaving it entirely alone is also unsafe, because unofficial cheat sheets are unversioned and silently carry outdated content, so the appropriate response is to make the sanctioned resource fast enough that clinicians choose it.
rationales.eli10: One person cutting across the grass is one person. A worn dirt track across the lawn where hundreds of feet have gone is not hundreds of rule-breakers; it is a sidewalk built in the wrong place. Landscape designers call those desire paths, and the good ones pave them. A workaround that nearly everyone uses is a desire path telling you the official route does not fit the actual job.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: When a workaround is nearly universal rather than isolated, it is evidence about the design and not about the people: work-as-imagined does not match work-as-done. questions.stem: After repeated problems with a bedside device, a hospital responds by adding three more pop-up warning screens to the device and requiring all staff to re-read the policy. What would most likely happen?

options.text: Reliability would improve substantially, because staff now receive more frequent reminders at the point of use.
Alert fatigue would rise and staff would click past the warnings, leaving the underlying design unchanged.
Errors would drop mainly among newer staff, since experienced staff act from habit rather than reading prompts.
Errors would largely disappear, since each warning must be acknowledged before the task can continue.

rationales.whyCorrect: Warnings, policies, and retraining sit at the weak end of the intervention effectiveness hierarchy because they rely entirely on human vigilance and memory, both of which degrade under workload and repetition. Stacking additional low-specificity alerts produces alert fatigue, in which users dismiss prompts reflexively, including the small proportion that carry real information; a required click records acknowledgment but does not demonstrate that anyone read or processed the message. A durable fix requires stronger action such as simplifying the task, standardizing or replacing the equipment, or building in a constraint that blocks the unsafe action outright.
rationales.eli10: If a car chimed every time you touched anything, you would stop hearing the chimes within a week, including the one that means a door is open at highway speed. That is alert fatigue, and clicking 'OK' is not the same as reading. Adding warnings feels like action because it is visible and cheap, but attention is a finite resource, and real fixes change the machine or the task so the warning is not needed.
rationales.distractorAnalysis: Warnings, policies, and retraining sit at the weak end of the intervention effectiveness hierarchy because they rely entirely on human vigilance and memory, both of which degrade under workload and repetition. A durable fix requires stronger action such as simplifying the task, standardizing or replacing the equipment, or building in a constraint that blocks the unsafe action outright.
